subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Differentiate between hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia.
answer_html:
Introduction The normal fasting plasma glucose is about 70–100 mg/dl. Values below or above the normal range are called hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia.

Point Hypoglycaemia Hyperglycaemia
Meaning blood glucose below about 70 mg/dl blood glucose above normal – fasting ≥126 mg/dl or random ≥200 mg/dl suggests diabetes
Common causes excess insulin or oral drugs, missed meals, heavy exercise, alcohol, liver failure diabetes mellitus, stress, infections, steroids, excess glucose infusion
Onset sudden – minutes gradual – hours to days
Features sweating, tremor, palpitation, hunger, confusion, fits, coma thirst, frequent urination, dry skin, tiredness, blurred vision; ketoacidosis in severe cases
Skin cold and clammy warm and dry
Emergency care give glucose at once insulin and IV fluids as prescribed

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is HbA1c? Give its normal value and significance.
answer_html:
Definition HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) is haemoglobin to which glucose is attached non-enzymatically. Because red cells live about 120 days, HbA1c reflects the average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months.

Values

  • Normal: below 5.7%
  • Prediabetes: 5.7–6.4%
  • Diabetes: 6.5% or more
  • Treatment target for most diabetic patients: below about 7%

Significance

  1. Diagnosis of diabetes; monitoring of long-term glycaemic control (tested every 3 months)
  2. Not affected by a recent meal – no fasting needed
  3. Higher values mean greater risk of eye, kidney and nerve complications

Note: falsely low after blood loss or haemolysis; falsely high in iron-deficiency anaemia.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is gluconeogenesis? Name its substrates.
answer_html:
Definition Gluconeogenesis is the formation of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources. It takes place mainly in the liver (about 90%) and partly in the kidneys, especially during prolonged fasting.

Substrates

  1. Lactate – from muscles and red cells (Cori cycle)
  2. Glycerol – from breakdown of fats
  3. Glucogenic amino acids – mainly alanine and glutamine, from muscle protein
  4. Propionate – in ruminants; minor in humans

Key enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase.

Significance

  • Maintains blood glucose during fasting and starvation, as the brain and red cells depend on glucose
  • Stimulated by glucagon and cortisol; inhibited by insulin
  • Excess gluconeogenesis contributes to high blood sugar in diabetes

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Differentiate between glycogenesis and glycogenolysis.
answer_html:
Point Glycogenesis Glycogenolysis
Meaning formation of glycogen from glucose breakdown of glycogen to glucose
Main sites liver and skeletal muscle liver and skeletal muscle
Key enzyme glycogen synthase glycogen phosphorylase
When after meals (fed state) between meals, fasting, exercise, stress
Stimulated by insulin glucagon (liver) and adrenaline (liver and muscle)
Effect on blood glucose lowers it (stores glucose) raises it (liver releases glucose)

Note: muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so muscle glycogen supplies energy only to the muscle itself; liver glycogen maintains blood glucose.

Clinical note: inherited enzyme defects cause glycogen storage diseases – e.g. von Gierke's disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency) with fasting hypoglycaemia and an enlarged liver.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is the Cori cycle?
answer_html:
Definition The Cori cycle (lactic acid cycle) is the cycle in which lactate produced in muscle is carried to the liver, converted back to glucose, and the glucose returns to the muscle.

Steps

  1. During strenuous exercise, muscle breaks glucose down by anaerobic glycolysis to lactate
  2. Lactate passes into the blood and reaches the liver
  3. The liver converts lactate to glucose (gluconeogenesis)
  4. Glucose returns to the blood and is used again by muscle

Significance

  • Prevents accumulation of lactate (lactic acidosis) and recycles it
  • It costs energy – the liver uses 6 ATP to make the glucose that gives muscle only 2 ATP
  • In liver failure and shock, lactate cannot be cleared and lactic acidosis develops

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is gestational diabetes mellitus? How is it screened in India?
answer_html:
Definition Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is high blood glucose first detected during pregnancy.

Screening (national guideline, single-step test)

  • Every pregnant woman is tested at the first antenatal visit and again at 24–28 weeks
  • She is given 75 g oral glucose (in about 300 ml water) irrespective of the last meal
  • Plasma glucose is checked after 2 hours
  • A value of 140 mg/dl or more = GDM

Importance

  • Risks to the baby – large baby (macrosomia), birth injury, neonatal hypoglycaemia
  • Risks to the mother – pre-eclampsia, caesarean section and type 2 diabetes later in life

Management: diet, exercise and, if needed, metformin or insulin; regular blood glucose monitoring.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is lactose intolerance?
answer_html:
Definition Lactose intolerance is the inability to digest lactose (milk sugar) because of deficiency of the enzyme lactase in the small intestine.

Mechanism

  • Undigested lactose reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it, producing gas and acids and drawing water into the bowel

Features (after taking milk)

  • Bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramps and watery (osmotic) diarrhoea

Types

  1. Primary – gradual loss of lactase after childhood; common in adults
  2. Secondary – temporary, after gastroenteritis or other intestinal disease
  3. Congenital – rare

Management

  • Reduce milk; curd and buttermilk are better tolerated
  • Lactose-free milk; ensure calcium from other foods

Diagnosis: hydrogen breath test, lactose tolerance test, or improvement when milk is stopped.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates.
answer_html:
Introduction Dietary carbohydrates are mainly starch (cereals, potatoes), sucrose (sugar), lactose (milk) and cellulose (fibre). Before absorption they must be broken down to monosaccharides – glucose, galactose and fructose.

A. Digestion

1. Mouth

  • Salivary amylase (ptyalin) begins breaking starch into dextrins and maltose
  • Works at pH about 6.8; action is brief because food stays in the mouth only a short time

2. Stomach

  • Hydrochloric acid inactivates salivary amylase; no carbohydrate-digesting enzyme is secreted here
  • Some digestion continues inside the food bolus until acid penetrates it

3. Small intestine – main site

  • Pancreatic amylase breaks starch into maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins
  • Brush-border (intestinal) enzymes complete digestion:
    • maltase – maltose → glucose + glucose
    • isomaltase (α-dextrinase) – limit dextrins → glucose
    • sucrase – sucrose → glucose + fructose
    • lactase – lactose → glucose + galactose
  • Cellulose is not digested, as humans lack cellulase – it acts as dietary fibre

B. Absorption

  • Takes place mainly in the duodenum and jejunum
  • Glucose and galactose – absorbed by active transport with sodium through the SGLT1 carrier
  • Fructose – absorbed by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5
  • All three leave the intestinal cell through GLUT2 into the blood → portal vein → liver
  • Rate of absorption: galactose > glucose > fructose

C. Fate after absorption

  • The liver converts galactose and fructose to glucose
  • Glucose is used for energy, stored as glycogen or converted to fat

D. Applied aspects

  • Oral rehydration solution (ORS) – glucose helps sodium (and therefore water) absorption through SGLT1; this is why ORS works in diarrhoea
  • Lactose intolerance – lactase deficiency causes bloating and diarrhoea after milk
  • Dietary fibre prevents constipation and lowers blood cholesterol and sugar
  • Malabsorption in pancreatic disease or intestinal damage
  • Diabetic patients – complex carbohydrates (whole grains) are absorbed slowly and raise blood sugar gradually

E. Nursing points

  • Prepare and give ORS correctly in diarrhoea – the glucose in it is essential for sodium and water absorption
  • Advise diabetic patients to prefer whole grains, pulses and vegetables over refined sugar and maida
  • Encourage fibre and fluids to prevent constipation in bedridden patients
  • In children with diarrhoea who develop bloating after milk, report possible secondary lactose intolerance

Conclusion Carbohydrate digestion begins with salivary amylase, is continued by pancreatic amylase and completed by brush-border enzymes; the resulting glucose, galactose and fructose are absorbed by SGLT1, GLUT5 and GLUT2 into the portal blood.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Describe the Krebs (TCA) cycle and its significance.
answer_html:
Introduction The Krebs cycle, also called the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle or citric acid cycle, is a series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix in which acetyl CoA is completely oxidised to CO₂ and water, releasing energy. It was described by Sir Hans Krebs.

1. Entry into the cycle

  • Acetyl CoA comes from carbohydrates (pyruvate), fats (fatty acids) and some amino acids
  • It combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C)

2. Steps of the cycle

  1. Acetyl CoA + oxaloacetate → citrate (citrate synthase)
  2. Citrate → isocitrate (aconitase)
  3. Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (isocitrate dehydrogenase) – NADH and CO₂ produced
  4. α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA (α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) – NADH and CO₂ produced
  5. Succinyl CoA → succinate – GTP (ATP) produced
  6. Succinate → fumarate (succinate dehydrogenase) – FADH₂ produced
  7. Fumarate → malate (fumarase)
  8. Malate → oxaloacetate (malate dehydrogenase) – NADH produced; oxaloacetate is regenerated

3. Energy yield per acetyl CoA

  • 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂
  • Through the electron transport chain this gives about 10 ATP (older textbooks: 12 ATP)

4. Vitamins needed

  • Thiamine (B₁), riboflavin (B₂ – FAD), niacin (B₃ – NAD), pantothenic acid (B₅ – coenzyme A) and lipoic acid
  • So deficiency of B vitamins reduces energy production (e.g. beriberi in thiamine deficiency)

5. Significance

  • Final common pathway for the oxidation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins
  • Produces most of the body's energy (ATP)
  • Amphibolic – it is both catabolic and anabolic; its intermediates are used to make glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and haem
  • Linked to the urea cycle through fumarate
  • Requires oxygen indirectly – the cycle stops when oxygen is lacking, as NADH cannot be reoxidised

6. Applied aspects

  • In hypoxia and shock, the cycle slows and cells depend on anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acidosis
  • Thiamine deficiency (alcoholics) → reduced energy and neurological damage
  • Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they cannot use the TCA cycle

7. Regulation

  • Key regulatory enzymes – citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
  • Slowed when the cell has plenty of energy (high ATP and NADH)
  • Speeded up when energy is needed (high ADP, calcium during muscle contraction)

Conclusion The Krebs cycle oxidises acetyl CoA in the mitochondria to CO₂, producing NADH, FADH₂ and GTP; it is the final common pathway of metabolism and the main source of the body's energy.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain glycolysis and its clinical significance.
answer_html:
Introduction Glycolysis (Embden–Meyerhof pathway) is the breakdown of one molecule of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate, with a small production of energy. It occurs in the cytoplasm of all cells and can take place with or without oxygen.

1. Phases

a. Energy investment phase

  • Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase; 1 ATP used)
  • Fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase-1; 1 ATP used) – the rate-limiting step
  • The 6-carbon sugar splits into two 3-carbon molecules (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate)

b. Energy generation phase

  • Each glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is oxidised, producing NADH
  • ATP is formed at two steps (substrate-level phosphorylation)
  • The last step, phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate, is catalysed by pyruvate kinase

2. Energy yield

  • Net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose
  • Aerobic conditions – pyruvate enters the mitochondria, forms acetyl CoA and is oxidised in the TCA cycle; complete oxidation of glucose gives about 30–32 ATP
  • Anaerobic conditions – pyruvate is converted to lactate (lactate dehydrogenase); only 2 ATP per glucose

3. Regulation

  • Key enzymes: hexokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase
  • Insulin stimulates glycolysis; glucagon inhibits it in the liver

4. Significance

  • The only energy source for red blood cells, which have no mitochondria
  • Gives quick energy to muscles during intense exercise
  • Provides energy when oxygen is short (hypoxia)
  • Its intermediates are used to make glycerol, amino acids and 2,3-BPG (which helps red cells release oxygen)

5. Clinical significance

  • Lactic acidosis – in shock, severe anaemia and cardiac arrest, tissues depend on anaerobic glycolysis and lactate accumulates
  • Pyruvate kinase deficiency – red cells lack energy → haemolytic anaemia
  • Fluoride inhibits a glycolytic enzyme (enolase) – that is why blood for glucose estimation is collected in fluoride (grey-top) tubes, to stop red cells using up the glucose
  • Cancer cells use glycolysis heavily

6. Aerobic versus anaerobic glycolysis

Point Aerobic Anaerobic
Oxygen present absent or short
End product pyruvate (enters mitochondria) lactate
NADH reoxidised in the electron transport chain reoxidised by converting pyruvate to lactate
Net ATP from glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH (more ATP later) 2 ATP only
Seen in most tissues at rest exercising muscle, red cells, hypoxic tissues

7. Nursing relevance

  • Collect blood for glucose in a fluoride tube and send it promptly
  • In shocked or hypoxic patients, a rising serum lactate warns of poor tissue oxygenation – report it
  • Muscle cramps and fatigue after heavy exercise are linked to lactate build-up

Conclusion Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm, yielding a net 2 ATP; it is the only energy source of red cells, supplies muscle during exercise and explains lactic acidosis in hypoxia.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Describe the glucose tolerance test – indications, procedure, interpretation and types of GTT curves.
answer_html:
Introduction The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) measures the body's ability to handle a standard glucose load. It is used when fasting or random values are borderline.

1. Indications

  • Borderline fasting or random blood glucose
  • Screening and diagnosis of gestational diabetes
  • Persons with glucose in urine but normal fasting glucose (to detect renal glycosuria)
  • Strong family history, obesity, recurrent infections, large babies in earlier pregnancies

2. Preparation

  • Normal diet with adequate carbohydrate (about 150 g/day) for 3 days before
  • Overnight fast of 8–12 hours; water allowed
  • No smoking, tea or exercise on the day of the test; stop interfering drugs if advised

3. Procedure (standard two-sample test)

  1. Collect a fasting blood sample (and urine)
  2. Give 75 g of glucose (anhydrous) dissolved in about 250–300 ml of water, to be drunk within 5 minutes; children 1.75 g/kg (maximum 75 g)
  3. Collect blood 2 hours later (in the classical test, samples are taken every 30 minutes for 2 hours, with urine samples)
  4. The patient remains seated and at rest and takes nothing by mouth except water

4. Interpretation (venous plasma glucose)

Status Fasting 2 hours after glucose
Normal below 100 mg/dl below 140 mg/dl
Impaired fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dl –
Impaired glucose tolerance – 140–199 mg/dl
Diabetes mellitus 126 mg/dl or more 200 mg/dl or more

5. Types of GTT curves

  • Normal curve – peak below about 160 mg/dl within an hour, back to normal by 2 hours; no glucose in urine
  • Diabetic curve – high fasting value, high peak (above 200 mg/dl), slow return; glucose in urine
  • Lag storage curve – very high early peak with glycosuria, then rapid fall, sometimes to hypoglycaemia; seen after gastrectomy, in hyperthyroidism and liver disease
  • Flat curve – very little rise; seen in malabsorption, hypothyroidism and Addison's disease
  • Renal glycosuria – normal blood curve but glucose in urine (low renal threshold)

6. Variations

  • Mini GTT – only fasting and 2-hour samples after 75 g glucose
  • Extended GTT – samples up to 5–6 hours, for suspected reactive hypoglycaemia
  • Glucose challenge test (GCT) – 50 g glucose without fasting; a 1-hour value above 140 mg/dl needs a full OGTT
  • Intravenous GTT – when oral glucose cannot be absorbed (malabsorption, after gastric surgery)

7. Nursing responsibilities

  • Explain the procedure and preparation; check fasting
  • Give the glucose drink correctly; note the exact times; label samples
  • Watch for nausea, vomiting (the test must be repeated if the patient vomits) and hypoglycaemia
  • Give food after the last sample

Conclusion The OGTT measures glucose handling after a 75 g load; fasting ≥126 mg/dl or 2-hour ≥200 mg/dl indicates diabetes, and curve patterns help detect impaired tolerance, malabsorption and renal glycosuria.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define diabetes mellitus. Explain its types, clinical features and complications.
answer_html:
Introduction Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterised by high blood glucose (hyperglycaemia) due to deficiency of insulin, resistance to its action, or both. It also disturbs fat and protein metabolism. India has one of the largest numbers of people with diabetes in the world.

1. Diagnosis

  • Fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dl, or
  • 2-hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dl in OGTT, or
  • HbA1c ≥6.5%, or
  • Random glucose ≥200 mg/dl with classical symptoms

2. Types

  1. Type 1 DM – autoimmune destruction of β-cells → absolute insulin deficiency; usually in children and young adults; prone to ketoacidosis; needs insulin for life
  2. Type 2 DM – insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency; adults, often obese, family history; about 90% of cases; treated with lifestyle changes, oral drugs and sometimes insulin
  3. Gestational DM – first detected in pregnancy
  4. Other specific types – diseases of the pancreas (pancreatitis), drugs (steroids), hormonal disorders (Cushing's syndrome), genetic forms

3. Clinical features

  • Polyuria (glucose in urine draws water), polydipsia (thirst), polyphagia (hunger)
  • Weight loss (type 1), tiredness, blurred vision
  • Frequent infections – boils, urinary and genital infections; slow wound healing
  • Tingling and numbness of feet

4. Biochemical changes

  • High blood glucose; glycosuria when blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (about 180 mg/dl)
  • Increased breakdown of fat → ketone bodies → ketonuria, ketoacidosis
  • Raised triglycerides and cholesterol

5. Complications

  • Acute:
    • diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) – mainly type 1
    • hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state – mainly type 2
    • hypoglycaemia – due to treatment
  • Chronic:
    • microvascular – retinopathy (blindness), nephropathy (kidney failure), neuropathy (loss of sensation, foot ulcers)
    • macrovascular – coronary artery disease, stroke, peripheral vascular disease
    • diabetic foot, infections, cataract

6. Management in brief

  • Diet – controlled calories, complex carbohydrates, high fibre, regular meals
  • Exercise and weight control
  • Drugs – metformin and other oral drugs; insulin
  • Monitoring – blood glucose, HbA1c every 3 months, urine albumin, eye and foot examination
  • Education – foot care, recognising hypoglycaemia, sick-day rules

7. Nursing role

  • Teach self-monitoring of blood glucose, correct insulin injection technique and site rotation
  • Daily foot inspection, proper footwear, nail care; never walk barefoot
  • Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia; carry sugar and an identity card
  • Encourage regular follow-up for eye, kidney and foot examination

Conclusion Diabetes mellitus is chronic hyperglycaemia due to insulin deficiency or resistance; its main types are type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes, and good control prevents its serious acute and chronic complications.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define hypoglycaemia. Describe its causes, features and management.
answer_html:
Definition Hypoglycaemia is a blood glucose level below about 70 mg/dl, usually with symptoms. A level below 54 mg/dl is clinically significant and dangerous. The brain depends on glucose, so severe hypoglycaemia is an emergency.

Whipple's triad: (1) symptoms of hypoglycaemia, (2) low blood glucose at the time, (3) relief of symptoms after glucose.

A. Causes

1. In diabetic patients (commonest)

  • Overdose of insulin or oral drugs (sulphonylureas)
  • Missed or delayed meals, vomiting
  • Unusual exercise
  • Alcohol
  • Kidney failure (drugs accumulate)

2. Fasting hypoglycaemia in non-diabetics

  • Prolonged starvation, severe malnutrition
  • Liver failure – poor glycogen stores and gluconeogenesis
  • Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), hypopituitarism
  • Insulinoma – an insulin-secreting tumour of the pancreas
  • Severe infections (sepsis), malaria (and its treatment with quinine)

3. Reactive (after meals)

  • After gastric surgery (dumping); early type 2 diabetes

4. In newborns

  • Babies of diabetic mothers, preterm and low-birth-weight babies, hypothermia, sepsis

5. Inborn errors

  • Glycogen storage diseases, galactosaemia

B. Features

  • Adrenergic (warning) signs – sweating, tremor, palpitation, hunger, anxiety, pallor
  • Neuroglycopenic signs – headache, confusion, abnormal behaviour, slurred speech, fits, coma
  • Elderly patients and those on beta-blockers may have few warning signs

C. Management

  • Conscious patient – "rule of 15":
    • give 15 g of fast-acting sugar (3 teaspoons of sugar in water, glucose tablets or half a glass of fruit juice)
    • recheck after 15 minutes; repeat if still low
    • then give a snack with complex carbohydrate
  • Unconscious patient:
    • nothing by mouth
    • IV dextrose (e.g. 25% or 50% dextrose) or glucagon 1 mg IM as ordered
    • recovery position; monitor blood glucose
  • Find and correct the cause (adjust insulin dose, regular meals)

D. Nursing points

  • Teach diabetic patients to carry sugar and recognise warning signs
  • Check blood glucose before giving insulin; ensure meals are served on time

E. Prevention

  • Regular meals and snacks; extra carbohydrate before exercise
  • Correct insulin technique and dose; do not inject and then skip a meal
  • Avoid alcohol on an empty stomach
  • Regular self-monitoring of blood glucose, especially in the elderly and those on sulphonylureas
  • Newborns at risk – early and frequent breastfeeding, keep warm, check blood glucose

Conclusion Hypoglycaemia (blood glucose below 70 mg/dl) is most often caused by diabetes treatment, missed meals or alcohol, and also by liver failure, adrenal insufficiency, insulinoma and starvation; it needs immediate glucose.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define lipids and give their classification.
answer_html:
Definition Lipids are organic compounds that are insoluble in water but soluble in fat solvents (ether, chloroform) and are related to fatty acids.

Classification (Bloor)

  1. Simple lipids – esters of fatty acids with alcohols
    • fats and oils (triacylglycerols)
    • waxes
  2. Compound lipids – contain additional groups
    • phospholipids (lecithin, cephalin, sphingomyelin)
    • glycolipids (cerebrosides, gangliosides)
    • lipoproteins
  3. Derived lipids – obtained by breakdown of the above
    • fatty acids, glycerol, steroids (cholesterol), ketone bodies, fat-soluble vitamins
  4. Miscellaneous – carotenoids, squalene

Functions in brief: energy store, cell membranes, hormones, insulation and protection of organs.

Examples of storage and structural lipids: triglycerides in adipose tissue; phospholipids and cholesterol in cell membranes.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Classify fatty acids with examples.
answer_html:
Definition Fatty acids are long-chain carboxylic acids that form the main part of most lipids.

Classification

  1. By saturation
    • Saturated – no double bonds: palmitic, stearic acid (ghee, coconut oil, animal fat)
    • Monounsaturated (MUFA) – one double bond: oleic acid (groundnut, mustard and olive oil)
    • Polyunsaturated (PUFA) – two or more double bonds: linoleic (ω-6), α-linolenic (ω-3), arachidonic acid, EPA, DHA (fish)
  2. By chain length – short-chain (below 6 carbons), medium-chain (6–12), long-chain (above 12)
  3. By need in the diet
    • Essential – cannot be made by the body: linoleic and α-linolenic acid
    • Non-essential – made in the body
  4. By shape – cis (natural) and trans (formed in hydrogenated fats)

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What are ketone bodies? Name them.
answer_html:
Definition Ketone bodies are water-soluble compounds produced in the liver from acetyl CoA when fat is broken down rapidly, as in carbohydrate shortage.

The three ketone bodies

  1. Acetoacetic acid (acetoacetate)
  2. β-hydroxybutyric acid – the most abundant
  3. Acetone – excreted through the lungs (fruity breath)

Use: an important fuel for the heart, muscles and, during starvation, the brain.

Conditions causing ketosis

  • Uncontrolled type 1 diabetes (diabetic ketoacidosis)
  • Starvation and prolonged fasting
  • Persistent vomiting, especially in children and in pregnancy (hyperemesis)
  • Very low-carbohydrate diets

Tests: urine dipstick or Rothera's test for ketones.

Normal blood level: below about 1 mg/dl (traces); they are not normally detected in urine.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the compounds formed from cholesterol.
answer_html:
Introduction Cholesterol is a steroid made mainly in the liver (and also taken in animal foods). It is the parent compound of several important substances.

Compounds formed from cholesterol

  1. Bile acids and bile salts (cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid) – digestion and absorption of fats; the main route of cholesterol excretion
  2. Steroid hormones
    • cortisol (glucocorticoid) and aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) – adrenal cortex
    • testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone – sex hormones
  3. Vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) – formed in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol by sunlight
  4. Cell membranes – cholesterol itself is a structural part of all cell membranes and myelin

Importance: although excess blood cholesterol is harmful, a certain amount is essential for these vital compounds.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is fatty liver? Give its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Fatty liver is the abnormal accumulation of fat (mainly triglycerides) in liver cells, more than about 5% of liver weight. Untreated, it may progress to inflammation, fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Causes

  1. Alcohol – the commonest cause in many patients
  2. Obesity, diabetes and high triglycerides – non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
  3. Protein deficiency (kwashiorkor) – the liver cannot make the proteins needed to export fat as VLDL
  4. Deficiency of lipotropic factors – choline, methionine
  5. Drugs and toxins – steroids, some antiviral drugs, carbon tetrachloride
  6. Starvation, pregnancy (rare acute fatty liver)

Prevention: avoid alcohol, control weight and diabetes, adequate protein.

Diagnosis: ultrasound of the abdomen (bright liver), raised ALT, liver biopsy in doubtful cases.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define lipoproteins. Explain their types and functions.

diagram.caption: Structure of a lipoprotein
labels: core of triglyceride and cholesterol ester

answer_html:
Definition Lipoproteins are complexes of lipids and proteins that transport lipids in the blood. Since lipids do not dissolve in water, they are packed inside a coat of phospholipids, free cholesterol and proteins called apolipoproteins.

Structure

  • Core: triglycerides and cholesterol esters (water-insoluble)
  • Surface: phospholipids, free cholesterol and apolipoproteins (water-soluble)

Types and functions

1. Chylomicrons

  • Largest and least dense; made in the intestine
  • Carry dietary (exogenous) triglycerides from the intestine through the lymph to tissues
  • Make plasma milky after a fatty meal

2. Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL)

  • Made in the liver
  • Carries triglycerides made in the liver (endogenous) to muscle and adipose tissue

3. Intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL)

  • Formed from VLDL; converted to LDL

4. Low-density lipoprotein (LDL)

  • Carries cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues
  • Excess LDL deposits cholesterol in artery walls → atherosclerosis – the "bad cholesterol"
  • Desirable LDL: below 100 mg/dl

5. High-density lipoprotein (HDL)

  • Made in the liver and intestine
  • Reverse cholesterol transport – collects excess cholesterol from tissues and arteries and brings it back to the liver for excretion
  • Protects against heart disease – the "good cholesterol"
  • Desirable HDL: above 40 mg/dl in men and 50 mg/dl in women

Comparison

Lipoprotein Made in Main lipid Function
Chylomicron intestine dietary triglyceride transport of dietary fat
VLDL liver endogenous triglyceride transport of liver-made fat
LDL from VLDL cholesterol cholesterol to tissues
HDL liver, intestine cholesterol, phospholipid cholesterol back to liver

Apolipoproteins

  • Act as structural proteins, enzyme activators and receptor recognition signals – e.g. apo B-100 (LDL), apo A-I (HDL), apo C-II (activates lipoprotein lipase)

Clinical importance

  • High LDL and low HDL increase the risk of coronary artery disease and stroke
  • Very high triglycerides can cause acute pancreatitis
  • Exercise, weight loss and avoiding trans fats raise HDL and lower LDL

Lipoprotein (a) – an LDL-like particle; high levels are inherited and increase the risk of early heart attack.

Nursing points

  • Collect the sample after a 12-hour fast for accurate triglyceride values
  • Teach patients the meaning of "good" (HDL) and "bad" (LDL) cholesterol and how exercise, diet and stopping smoking improve them

Conclusion Lipoproteins transport lipids in blood: chylomicrons and VLDL carry triglycerides, LDL carries cholesterol to tissues and HDL returns it to the liver; their balance determines the risk of atherosclerosis.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define phospholipids. Give examples of common phospholipids with their functions.
answer_html:
Definition Phospholipids are compound lipids that contain, besides fatty acids and an alcohol, a phosphoric acid group and usually a nitrogenous base. They have a water-loving (hydrophilic) head and water-hating (hydrophobic) tails, so they form double layers (bilayers) – the basis of cell membranes.

A. Types and examples

1. Glycerophospholipids (alcohol = glycerol)

  • Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) – the most abundant; in membranes, bile and lung surfactant
  • Cephalin (phosphatidylethanolamine) – in membranes; helps blood clotting
  • Phosphatidylserine – in platelet membranes; takes part in clotting
  • Phosphatidylinositol – source of second messengers
  • Cardiolipin – in the inner mitochondrial membrane
  • Plasmalogens – in heart and brain

2. Sphingophospholipids (alcohol = sphingosine)

  • Sphingomyelin – in the myelin sheath of nerves

B. Functions

  1. Structure of cell membranes – the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves cells
  2. Lung surfactant – dipalmitoyl lecithin lowers surface tension in the alveoli and prevents their collapse; its deficiency in preterm babies causes respiratory distress syndrome
  3. Myelin sheath – sphingomyelin insulates nerve fibres for fast conduction
  4. Blood clotting – platelet phospholipids (phosphatidylserine, cephalin) provide the surface for clotting factors
  5. Lipoprotein structure – form the outer coat of lipoproteins that carry fats in blood
  6. Bile – lecithin keeps cholesterol dissolved in bile and helps emulsify fats
  7. Cell signalling – phosphatidylinositol forms IP₃ and DAG, second messengers for hormones
  8. Source of arachidonic acid for prostaglandins

C. Clinical importance

  • Lecithin–sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio in amniotic fluid above 2 indicates fetal lung maturity
  • Antenatal steroids given to mothers in preterm labour increase surfactant production
  • Low lecithin in bile favours gallstone formation
  • Lipid storage diseases (e.g. Niemann–Pick disease – sphingomyelin accumulates)

D. Nursing relevance

  • Preterm labour – give antenatal corticosteroids on time as ordered to mature the baby's lungs
  • Preterm babies with breathing difficulty may receive surfactant through the endotracheal tube; monitor oxygen saturation and breathing after it
  • Patients with fat malabsorption or on fat-free diets may lack essential fatty acids needed for phospholipids – report skin changes
  • Explain to antenatal mothers why steroid injections are given in preterm labour

Conclusion Phospholipids such as lecithin, cephalin, phosphatidylserine and sphingomyelin form cell membranes, lung surfactant and myelin and take part in clotting, fat transport and cell signalling.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the digestion and absorption of lipids.
answer_html:
Introduction Most dietary fat is triglyceride (triacylglycerol), with small amounts of cholesterol and phospholipids. Because fats do not mix with water, their digestion needs emulsification by bile before enzymes can act.

A. Digestion

1. Mouth and stomach

  • Lingual and gastric lipases digest a small amount of fat – more important in infants (milk fat)

2. Small intestine – main site

  • Emulsification – bile salts from the liver break large fat globules into tiny droplets, increasing the surface area for enzymes
  • Pancreatic lipase (with colipase) splits triglycerides into 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids
  • Cholesterol esterase – cholesterol esters → cholesterol + fatty acids
  • Phospholipase A₂ – phospholipids → lysophospholipids + fatty acids

B. Absorption

  1. The products combine with bile salts to form tiny micelles, which carry them to the surface of intestinal cells
  2. They diffuse into the intestinal cells (enterocytes); bile salts stay behind and are later reabsorbed in the ileum (enterohepatic circulation)
  3. Inside the cells, fatty acids and monoacylglycerol are re-formed into triglycerides
  4. Triglycerides, cholesterol and phospholipids are packed with protein into chylomicrons
  5. Chylomicrons enter the lacteals (lymph vessels) → thoracic duct → blood
  6. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are absorbed directly into the portal blood

C. Fate

  • In tissues, lipoprotein lipase releases fatty acids from chylomicrons for energy or storage in adipose tissue

D. Applied aspects

  • Steatorrhoea (bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools) occurs when fat is not digested or absorbed:
    • obstructive jaundice (no bile reaches the intestine)
    • pancreatitis and cystic fibrosis (lack of lipase)
    • intestinal diseases (coeliac disease)
  • Deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) in fat malabsorption – e.g. bleeding due to vitamin K deficiency
  • Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil is given in malabsorption, as it is absorbed directly
  • Anti-obesity drug orlistat works by blocking lipase

E. Nursing points

  • Observe and record stool character – pale, bulky, greasy, floating stools suggest fat malabsorption
  • Patients with obstructive jaundice may need vitamin K before surgery or procedures
  • Give pancreatic enzyme supplements with meals as prescribed in pancreatic insufficiency
  • After cholecystectomy, advise a low-fat diet at first and gradual reintroduction of fat

Conclusion Fats are emulsified by bile salts, digested mainly by pancreatic lipase, absorbed through micelles, re-formed into triglycerides and carried as chylomicrons through the lymph into the blood.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the clinical significance of MUFA, PUFA, essential fatty acids and trans fatty acids.
answer_html:
Introduction The type of fat in the diet affects blood lipids, heart health, inflammation and growth. Fatty acids are grouped as saturated, monounsaturated (MUFA), polyunsaturated (PUFA) and trans fatty acids.

1. Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA)

  • One double bond – mainly oleic acid
  • Sources: groundnut, mustard, rice bran, olive and canola oils; nuts
  • Significance: lower LDL while maintaining HDL; reduce the risk of heart disease; part of a heart-healthy diet

2. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)

  • Two or more double bonds
  • Omega-6 (ω-6) – linoleic acid: sunflower, safflower, corn, soybean oils
  • Omega-3 (ω-3) – α-linolenic acid (flaxseed/alsi, mustard oil, soybean, walnuts, green leafy vegetables) and EPA and DHA (fish, fish oil)
  • Significance:
    • lower blood cholesterol and triglycerides (especially ω-3)
    • ω-3 fats are anti-inflammatory, reduce clotting and irregular heart rhythms
    • DHA is essential for development of the brain and retina – important in pregnancy, lactation and infancy
    • a balanced ω-6 : ω-3 ratio is needed; Indian diets often have too much ω-6
    • PUFA oils are easily oxidised – do not reheat repeatedly

3. Essential fatty acids (EFA)

  • Linoleic and α-linolenic acids cannot be made by the body and must come from the diet; arachidonic acid is made from linoleic acid
  • Functions: structure of cell membranes, formation of prostaglandins and related compounds, healthy skin, transport of cholesterol, brain development
  • Deficiency: phrynoderma (rough "toad skin"), dermatitis, poor wound healing, poor growth, fatty liver – seen in severe malnutrition and in patients on fat-free parenteral nutrition

4. Trans fatty acids

  • Formed when vegetable oils are partially hydrogenated (vanaspati, some margarines) and during repeated deep frying; small amounts in dairy and meat
  • Harmful effects:
    • raise LDL and lower HDL – the worst combination
    • increase inflammation and the risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and diabetes
  • In India, FSSAI limits trans fat to not more than 2% in edible oils and fats

5. Dietary advice

  • Use a mix of oils (e.g. groundnut or mustard with sunflower or rice bran) to balance MUFA, ω-6 and ω-3
  • Limit saturated fats (ghee, butter, coconut oil) and avoid vanaspati and reheated oil
  • Include ω-3 sources – flaxseed, walnuts, green leafy vegetables, fish
  • Total visible fat about 20–30 g a day for adults (as per Indian dietary guidelines)

Conclusion MUFA and PUFA, especially ω-3 fatty acids, protect the heart and support brain development; essential fatty acids must come from food; trans fatty acids raise LDL, lower HDL and should be avoided.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the formation of ketone bodies (ketogenesis) and the clinical significance of ketosis.
answer_html:
Introduction Ketone bodies – acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone – are produced in the liver when fatty acids are broken down faster than the TCA cycle can use the resulting acetyl CoA.

A. Ketogenesis (formation)

  • Site: liver mitochondria
  • Conditions: low insulin and high glucagon – fasting, starvation, uncontrolled diabetes
  • Steps in brief:
    1. Fat is broken down → fatty acids reach the liver → β-oxidation produces much acetyl CoA
    2. Oxaloacetate is used up for gluconeogenesis, so acetyl CoA cannot all enter the TCA cycle
    3. Two acetyl CoA → acetoacetyl CoA → HMG CoA → acetoacetate
    4. Acetoacetate → β-hydroxybutyrate; part changes spontaneously to acetone

B. Utilisation (ketolysis)

  • Ketone bodies pass into the blood and are used for energy by the heart, skeletal muscle, kidney and, in prolonged starvation, the brain
  • The liver cannot use ketone bodies, because it lacks the enzyme needed to activate acetoacetate

C. Ketosis

  • When production exceeds use: ketonaemia (in blood) + ketonuria (in urine) = ketosis
  • Causes:
    • uncontrolled type 1 diabetes
    • starvation and prolonged fasting
    • persistent vomiting (children, hyperemesis gravidarum)
    • very low-carbohydrate diets, alcoholism

D. Clinical significance – diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

  • Ketone bodies are acids → metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap
  • Features:
    • fruity (acetone) smell of breath
    • deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing
    • nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
    • dehydration from glucose-induced diuresis
    • drowsiness and coma
  • Investigations: high blood glucose, ketones in blood and urine, low pH and bicarbonate on ABG, potassium changes
  • Treatment: IV fluids, insulin, potassium replacement, treat the trigger (often infection or missed insulin)

E. Nursing points

  • Test urine or blood for ketones in diabetic patients who are ill or vomiting
  • Monitor blood glucose, ketones, potassium, intake–output and level of consciousness in DKA
  • Teach "sick-day rules" – never stop insulin during illness; drink fluids; check ketones

F. Starvation ketosis versus diabetic ketoacidosis

Point Starvation ketosis Diabetic ketoacidosis
Blood glucose normal or low very high (often above 250 mg/dl)
Insulin low but present absent or very low
Ketone level mild very high
Acidosis mild or absent severe (pH below 7.3)
Treatment carbohydrate feeding IV fluids, insulin, potassium

Conclusion Ketone bodies are made in liver mitochondria from excess acetyl CoA during carbohydrate shortage and are used by extrahepatic tissues; their excess causes ketosis and, in uncontrolled diabetes, life-threatening ketoacidosis.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the metabolism of cholesterol and its clinical importance.
answer_html:
Introduction Cholesterol is a steroid alcohol present in all animal cells. It is obtained from the diet (eggs, meat, ghee, butter) and made in the body, mainly in the liver (about 1 g a day). Plant foods contain no cholesterol.

A. Synthesis

  • Site: liver (also intestine, adrenal cortex, gonads, skin) – in the cytoplasm
  • Starting material: acetyl CoA
  • Pathway in brief: acetyl CoA → HMG CoA → mevalonate → isoprene units → squalene → lanosterol → cholesterol
  • Rate-limiting enzyme: HMG CoA reductase
  • Regulation:
    • inhibited by high cholesterol intake (feedback), glucagon and statin drugs
    • stimulated by insulin and diets rich in saturated fat

B. Transport

  • Carried in blood by lipoproteins – LDL to tissues and HDL back to the liver

C. Uses (fate)

  1. Cell membranes and myelin
  2. Bile acids – the major route of breakdown
  3. Steroid hormones – cortisol, aldosterone, sex hormones
  4. Vitamin D₃ in the skin

D. Excretion

  • The body cannot break down the steroid ring; cholesterol is removed through bile, as free cholesterol and as bile acids, in the faeces
  • Dietary fibre binds bile acids and increases their excretion – lowering blood cholesterol

E. Normal value

  • Total serum cholesterol: desirable below 200 mg/dl

F. Clinical importance

  • Hypercholesterolaemia – high LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis, coronary heart disease, stroke
    • causes: diet rich in saturated and trans fats, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, obstructive jaundice, familial hypercholesterolaemia
  • Gallstones – excess cholesterol in bile crystallises
  • Xanthomas – yellow deposits in skin and tendons in very high cholesterol
  • Low cholesterol – in hyperthyroidism, malnutrition, liver failure

G. Lowering blood cholesterol

  • Diet low in saturated and trans fats, high in fibre, fruits and vegetables; use of MUFA/PUFA oils
  • Exercise, weight reduction, no smoking
  • Drugs – statins (block HMG CoA reductase), ezetimibe (blocks absorption), bile acid binders

H. Nursing points

  • Teach a low saturated-fat, high-fibre diet; limit egg yolk, organ meat, ghee and fried foods
  • Statins are usually taken at night (cholesterol synthesis is highest at night); report muscle pain (a side effect)
  • Encourage regular exercise and periodic lipid profile tests

Conclusion Cholesterol is made from acetyl CoA in the liver under the control of HMG CoA reductase, is used for membranes, bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D, and is excreted only through bile; excess LDL cholesterol leads to atherosclerosis.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the lipid profile – its components, normal values and interpretation.
answer_html:
Introduction A lipid profile is a group of blood tests that measures the fats in the blood. It is used to assess the risk of heart disease and stroke and to monitor treatment.

A. Components and desirable values (adults)

Test Desirable value
Total cholesterol below 200 mg/dl (200–239 borderline; 240 or above high)
Triglycerides below 150 mg/dl
HDL cholesterol above 40 mg/dl (men), above 50 mg/dl (women); 60 or above is protective
LDL cholesterol below 100 mg/dl (optimal); 160 or above high
VLDL cholesterol about triglycerides ÷ 5 (below 30 mg/dl)
Non-HDL cholesterol total cholesterol minus HDL; below 130 mg/dl
Total cholesterol : HDL ratio below 4.5
  • LDL is often calculated by the Friedewald formula: LDL = total cholesterol – HDL – (triglycerides ÷ 5), valid when triglycerides are below 400 mg/dl
  • Targets are lower for people with diabetes or heart disease, as advised by the doctor

B. Preparation and sample

  • Fasting for 9–12 hours (water allowed) is preferred, especially for triglycerides
  • Usual diet for the preceding weeks; avoid alcohol and heavy fatty meals the day before
  • Venous blood in a plain or gel tube

C. Interpretation

  • High total and LDL cholesterol – risk of atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease
  • Low HDL – increased risk even when total cholesterol is normal; common with smoking, obesity, inactivity, diabetes
  • High triglycerides – diabetes, obesity, alcohol, high sugar intake; very high values (above about 500–1,000 mg/dl) can cause acute pancreatitis

D. Causes of abnormal lipid profile (dyslipidaemia)

  • Primary – inherited (familial hypercholesterolaemia)
  • Secondary – diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, obesity, alcohol, obstructive jaundice, drugs (steroids, some diuretics)

E. Who should be tested

  • Adults periodically from about 20 years; people with diabetes, hypertension, obesity, smoking, family history of early heart disease

F. Nursing responsibilities

  • Explain fasting requirements; collect the sample correctly
  • Counsel on diet, exercise, weight control, quitting smoking and regular medicines (statins)

G. Factors that can affect the result

  • Recent meal (raises triglycerides), alcohol, acute illness or recent heart attack (cholesterol may fall temporarily), pregnancy
  • Drugs – steroids, oral contraceptives, beta-blockers, thiazides

Conclusion The lipid profile measures total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, LDL and VLDL; high LDL and triglycerides with low HDL indicate increased cardiovascular risk and call for lifestyle change and treatment.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain atherosclerosis – its causes, role of lipids, complications and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Atherosclerosis is a disease of large and medium-sized arteries in which lipids (mainly cholesterol), inflammatory cells and fibrous tissue are deposited in the inner wall (intima) to form plaques (atheromas). The plaques narrow the artery and may rupture, causing clots.

A. Risk factors

  • Non-modifiable – increasing age, male sex (women after menopause), family history
  • Modifiable:
    • high LDL cholesterol, low HDL, high triglycerides
    • smoking and tobacco use
    • hypertension
    • diabetes mellitus
    • obesity, especially abdominal
    • physical inactivity, unhealthy diet (saturated and trans fats), stress

B. Role of lipids in plaque formation

  1. Injury to the endothelium – by high BP, smoking, high glucose and LDL
  2. LDL enters the arterial wall and is oxidised
  3. Macrophages engulf oxidised LDL and become foam cells → fatty streak
  4. Smooth muscle cells grow and form a fibrous cap over a lipid core → mature plaque
  5. Plaque may rupture → platelets gather → thrombus blocks the artery - HDL protects by removing cholesterol from the arterial wall

C. Complications

  • Coronary artery disease – angina, myocardial infarction
  • Stroke – cerebral arteries
  • Peripheral arterial disease – pain on walking, gangrene
  • Aneurysm – weakening and bulging of the aorta
  • Renal artery stenosis – hypertension, kidney damage

D. Investigations

  • Lipid profile, blood glucose, HbA1c, ECG, echocardiography; angiography when needed

E. Prevention and management

  • Diet – less saturated fat, no trans fat, less salt and sugar; more fibre, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, ω-3 fats
  • Regular exercise (at least 30 minutes most days), weight control
  • Stop smoking; limit alcohol
  • Control BP, diabetes and cholesterol – statins, antihypertensives, antiplatelet drugs (aspirin) as prescribed

F. Nurse's role

  • Health education on heart-healthy lifestyle; screening of BP, sugar and lipids
  • Encourage adherence to medicines and follow-up

G. Common sites and warning signs

  • Coronary arteries – chest pain on exertion (angina), breathlessness
  • Carotid and cerebral arteries – transient weakness, speech difficulty (TIA), stroke
  • Leg arteries – pain in the calf on walking that is relieved by rest (claudication), cold feet, non-healing ulcers
  • Aorta – pulsating mass in the abdomen (aneurysm)
  • Early detection allows treatment before a heart attack or stroke occurs

Conclusion Atherosclerosis is the deposition of oxidised LDL cholesterol, foam cells and fibrous tissue in arterial walls, promoted by high LDL, smoking, hypertension and diabetes; it causes heart attacks and strokes and is largely preventable through lifestyle changes.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: List the essential amino acids.
answer_html:
Definition Essential amino acids are amino acids that cannot be made in the body (or not in enough quantity) and must be supplied by the diet.

Essential amino acids (mnemonic "PVT TIM HALL")

  1. Phenylalanine
  2. Valine
  3. Threonine
  4. Tryptophan
  5. Isoleucine
  6. Methionine
  7. Histidine
  8. Arginine – semi-essential: needed from food during growth, pregnancy and illness
  9. Leucine
  10. Lysine

Points to remember

  • Lysine is limited in cereals and methionine in pulses – so cereal + pulse combinations (dal–rice, khichdi) supply all essential amino acids
  • Lack of any essential amino acid stops protein synthesis and leads to negative nitrogen balance

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Write the causes of proteinuria.
answer_html:
Definition Proteinuria is the excretion of more than 150 mg of protein in urine per day.

Causes

  1. Physiological (transient) – heavy exercise, fever, exposure to cold, emotional stress, orthostatic (on standing) proteinuria in young people
  2. Pre-renal (overflow) – excess small proteins in blood: Bence Jones proteins (multiple myeloma), haemoglobin (haemolysis), myoglobin (crush injury)
  3. Renal – glomerular – glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome (more than 3.5 g/day), diabetic nephropathy, hypertension, pre-eclampsia
  4. Renal – tubular – pyelonephritis, heavy-metal poisoning, some drugs
  5. Post-renal – urinary tract infection, stones and tumours of the urinary tract (protein from pus and blood)

Tests: dipstick, heat coagulation test, 24-hour urine protein and urine albumin–creatinine ratio.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Differentiate between transamination and deamination.
answer_html:
Point Transamination Deamination
Meaning transfer of the amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid removal of the amino group as free ammonia
Products a new amino acid (usually glutamate) and a new keto acid ammonia + keto acid
Free ammonia not released released – goes to the urea cycle
Enzymes aminotransferases – ALT, AST glutamate dehydrogenase (oxidative deamination)
Coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B₆) NAD⁺ or NADP⁺ (niacin)
Site most tissues, mainly liver mainly liver and kidney
Significance synthesis of non-essential amino acids; collects amino groups as glutamate final release of nitrogen for urea formation

Note: the two act together (transdeamination) to remove nitrogen from most amino acids.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is phenylketonuria?
answer_html:
Definition Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inherited (autosomal recessive) disorder in which phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine because of deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase.

Biochemical changes

  • Phenylalanine accumulates in blood and is converted to phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate and phenylacetate, which appear in urine (phenylketones)

Features

  • Intellectual disability, fits, hyperactivity
  • Light skin, hair and eyes (less melanin), eczema
  • Mousy (musty) odour of urine and sweat

Diagnosis

  • Newborn screening of a heel-prick blood spot; ferric chloride test of urine gives a green colour

Treatment

  • Low-phenylalanine diet (special formula) started in the first weeks of life and continued long-term; avoid the sweetener aspartame

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is the albumin–globulin (A:G) ratio? Give its normal value and significance.
answer_html:
Definition The A:G ratio is the ratio of serum albumin to serum globulin.

Normal values

  • Total serum protein: 6–8 g/dl
  • Albumin: 3.5–5.0 g/dl; globulin: 2.0–3.5 g/dl
  • A:G ratio: about 1.2:1 to 2.5:1

Significance – reversed (low) A:G ratio occurs when albumin falls or globulin rises:

  1. Liver cirrhosis – liver makes less albumin; globulins rise
  2. Nephrotic syndrome – albumin is lost in urine
  3. Multiple myeloma – large increase of one globulin
  4. Chronic infections – tuberculosis, kala-azar, chronic hepatitis
  5. Autoimmune diseases – SLE, rheumatoid arthritis
  6. Malnutrition and malabsorption – low albumin

High A:G ratio is uncommon – seen in hypogammaglobulinaemia (low immunoglobulins).

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is hypoproteinaemia? Give its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Hypoproteinaemia is a total serum protein below 6 g/dl, usually due to low albumin (below 3.5 g/dl).

Causes

  1. Decreased intake – starvation, kwashiorkor, protein-energy malnutrition
  2. Decreased absorption – malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea
  3. Decreased synthesis – liver cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis
  4. Increased loss
    • kidney – nephrotic syndrome
    • skin – extensive burns
    • gut – protein-losing enteropathy
    • blood loss, repeated tapping of ascites
  5. Increased breakdown – fever, sepsis, major surgery, cancer
  6. Dilution – excess IV fluids, pregnancy

Effects: oedema and ascites (low oncotic pressure), poor wound healing, low resistance to infection.

Nursing points: weigh daily, look for pitting oedema and ascites, record intake–output, and encourage a high-protein diet unless restricted (as in kidney or liver failure with encephalopathy).

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is hypergammaglobulinaemia? Give its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Hypergammaglobulinaemia is an increase of gamma globulins (immunoglobulins) in the blood.

Types and causes

  1. Polyclonal – many clones of plasma cells produce antibodies; a broad band in electrophoresis
    • chronic infections – tuberculosis, kala-azar, malaria, HIV
    • chronic liver disease – cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis
    • autoimmune diseases – SLE, rheumatoid arthritis
  2. Monoclonal – a single clone of plasma cells; a sharp "M band"
    • multiple myeloma
    • Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia
    • monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS)

Effects: raised ESR, increased blood viscosity, reversed A:G ratio.

Diagnosis: serum protein electrophoresis (broad band or sharp spike in the gamma region), immunofixation and measurement of individual immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM).

Nursing: watch for signs of hyperviscosity in myeloma – headache, blurred vision, bleeding – and keep the patient well hydrated.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What are Bence Jones proteins?
answer_html:
Definition Bence Jones proteins are free light chains (kappa or lambda) of immunoglobulins produced in excess by a clone of plasma cells and excreted in urine.

Seen in

  • Multiple myeloma (about half to three-quarters of patients)
  • Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia, amyloidosis

Special heat property

  • On heating urine they precipitate at 40–60 °C, redissolve near boiling and reappear on cooling

Detection

  • Urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation (preferred)
  • The routine dipstick does not detect them well, as it reacts mainly with albumin

Significance

  • Diagnosis of myeloma; they damage the kidney tubules (myeloma kidney)

Nursing: send an early-morning or 24-hour urine sample as ordered and keep myeloma patients well hydrated to protect the kidneys.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the levels of structure of proteins.
answer_html:
Introduction Proteins are long chains of amino acids folded into a definite three-dimensional shape on which their function depends.

Levels of structure

  1. Primary structure – the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; decided by the gene
  2. Secondary structure – local folding into an α-helix or β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds (e.g. keratin, silk)
  3. Tertiary structure – three-dimensional folding of the whole chain, held by disulphide bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions (e.g. myoglobin)
  4. Quaternary structure – two or more polypeptide chains (subunits) joined together, e.g. haemoglobin (2 α + 2 β chains)

Note: denaturation destroys the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure but not the primary structure.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is a molecular disease? Explain with the example of sickle cell anaemia.
answer_html:
Definition A molecular disease is a disease caused by an abnormal protein molecule resulting from a gene mutation. Sickle cell anaemia was the first one described (Pauling).

Sickle cell anaemia

  • Point mutation in the β-globin gene: glutamic acid is replaced by valine at the 6th position of the β-chain → HbS
  • When oxygen is low, HbS molecules polymerise; red cells become sickle-shaped, rigid and fragile
  • Results – haemolytic anaemia, painful vaso-occlusive crises, infections, organ damage

Indian context

  • Common in tribal populations of central and western India, including the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra
  • The National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) provides screening, genetic counselling and care, aiming at elimination by 2047

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define amino acids. Classify them and list the factors causing denaturation of proteins.
answer_html:
A. Definition Amino acids are organic compounds that contain an amino group (–NH₂) and a carboxyl group (–COOH) attached to the same α-carbon, along with a side chain (R group). They are the building blocks of proteins; 20 standard amino acids are found in human proteins.

B. Classification

1. Based on the structure of the side chain

  • Aliphatic – glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine
  • Hydroxyl-containing – serine, threonine
  • Sulphur-containing – cysteine, methionine
  • Acidic and their amides – aspartic acid, glutamic acid; asparagine, glutamine
  • Basic – lysine, arginine, histidine
  • Aromatic – phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan
  • Imino acid – proline

2. Based on polarity

  • Non-polar (hydrophobic) – alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, proline
  • Polar, uncharged – glycine, serine, threonine, tyrosine, cysteine, asparagine, glutamine
  • Polar, charged – acidic (aspartate, glutamate) and basic (lysine, arginine, histidine)

3. Nutritional

  • Essential – must come from food (e.g. lysine, tryptophan, methionine)
  • Semi-essential – arginine (needed in growth)
  • Non-essential – made in the body (e.g. alanine, glycine, serine)

4. Metabolic (fate of the carbon skeleton)

  • Purely ketogenic – leucine, lysine
  • Both ketogenic and glucogenic – isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, threonine
  • Glucogenic – all the rest

C. Denaturation of proteins

  • Definition: loss of the natural three-dimensional shape (secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure) of a protein without breaking peptide bonds, resulting in loss of biological activity

Factors causing denaturation

  • Physical – heat (boiling an egg), UV and X-rays, high pressure, vigorous shaking, ultrasound
  • Chemical:
    • strong acids and alkalis (extremes of pH)
    • organic solvents – alcohol, acetone
    • heavy-metal salts – mercury, lead, silver
    • detergents, urea, reducing agents (break disulphide bonds)

Effects: loss of activity, decreased solubility (coagulation), increased digestibility.

D. Applied aspects

  • Cooking makes proteins easier to digest
  • 70% alcohol and autoclaving kill microbes by denaturing their proteins
  • Heat coagulation test detects albumin in urine
  • Milk or egg white is given in heavy-metal poisoning – the proteins bind the metal
  • Very high fever (above 41 °C) denatures body enzymes

E. Important properties of amino acids

  • Amphoteric – act as both acid and base, so they help in buffering
  • Exist as zwitterions (carry both + and – charges) at their isoelectric pH, where they have no net charge and are least soluble
  • All except glycine are optically active; human proteins contain L-amino acids
  • Join together by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–) to form peptides and proteins

Conclusion Amino acids are classified by structure, polarity, nutritional need and metabolic fate; heat, extremes of pH, alcohol and heavy metals denature proteins – a fact used in cooking, sterilisation and laboratory tests.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the digestion and absorption of proteins.
answer_html:
Introduction Dietary proteins come from pulses, milk, eggs, meat, fish and cereals. They are broken down to amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides before absorption. Protein-digesting enzymes are secreted as inactive forms (zymogens) so that they do not digest the glands that make them.

A. Digestion

1. Mouth – no protein digestion; food is only chewed and mixed

2. Stomach

  • Hydrochloric acid denatures proteins, kills microbes and converts pepsinogen → pepsin
  • Pepsin (endopeptidase) breaks proteins into proteoses, peptones and polypeptides
  • Pepsin also clots milk protein (casein) in infants

3. Small intestine – pancreatic enzymes

  • Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) of the intestinal mucosa converts trypsinogen → trypsin
  • Trypsin activates the other zymogens:
    • chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin
    • proelastase → elastase
    • procarboxypeptidase → carboxypeptidase
  • Endopeptidases (trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase) split peptide bonds inside the chain; exopeptidases (carboxypeptidase) remove amino acids from the end

4. Small intestine – brush-border enzymes

  • Aminopeptidases, dipeptidases and tripeptidases complete digestion to free amino acids and small peptides

B. Absorption

  • Takes place mainly in the jejunum and ileum
  • Free amino acids – sodium-dependent active transport, with separate carriers for neutral, acidic, basic and imino amino acids
  • Di- and tripeptides – absorbed by a peptide transporter and broken down inside the intestinal cells
  • Amino acids enter the portal blood and go to the liver
  • Newborns can absorb some intact proteins – antibodies from colostrum give passive immunity

C. Fate after absorption

  • Used to make body proteins, enzymes, hormones and other compounds; excess is broken down for energy and its nitrogen excreted as urea

D. Applied aspects

  • Pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis – poor protein digestion; undigested protein appears in stools
  • Acute pancreatitis – early activation of trypsin inside the pancreas causes self-digestion
  • Cystinuria and Hartnup disease – inherited defects of amino acid transport
  • Absorption of intact food proteins may cause food allergy in infants
  • Protein-losing enteropathy and malabsorption lead to hypoproteinaemia

E. Nursing points

  • Give pancreatic enzyme supplements with meals when prescribed
  • Encourage colostrum feeding of newborns
  • Ensure good-quality protein in the diet of convalescent, surgical and burn patients

Conclusion Protein digestion begins with pepsin in the stomach, continues with trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase from the pancreas and is completed by brush-border peptidases; amino acids are absorbed by active transport into the portal blood.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Describe the types and functions of plasma proteins with their normal values.
answer_html:
Introduction Plasma proteins are the proteins present in plasma. Most are made in the liver; immunoglobulins are made by plasma cells.

A. Normal values

  • Total protein: 6–8 g/dl
  • Albumin: 3.5–5.0 g/dl
  • Globulins: 2.0–3.5 g/dl
  • Fibrinogen: 200–400 mg/dl
  • A:G ratio: about 1.2–2.5 : 1

B. Types

  1. Albumin – the most abundant and smallest plasma protein
  2. Globulins – separated by electrophoresis into:
    • α₁ – α₁-antitrypsin, α₁-acid glycoprotein
    • α₂ – haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, α₂-macroglobulin
    • β – transferrin, LDL, complement C3
    • γ – immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE)
  3. Fibrinogen and other clotting factors (prothrombin)
  4. Others – C-reactive protein, prealbumin (transthyretin), hormones and enzymes

C. Functions

  1. Colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure – about 25 mmHg; albumin provides about 80%; it holds water inside blood vessels and prevents oedema
  2. Transport
    • albumin – bilirubin, free fatty acids, calcium, hormones and many drugs
    • transferrin – iron; ceruloplasmin – copper; haptoglobin – free haemoglobin
    • lipoproteins – lipids; thyroxine-binding globulin – thyroid hormones
  3. Defence – immunoglobulins (antibodies) and complement proteins
  4. Blood coagulation – fibrinogen, prothrombin and other clotting factors
  5. Buffering – plasma proteins help to keep blood pH constant
  6. Viscosity – contribute to the viscosity of blood and thus to blood pressure
  7. Nutrition – a reserve source of amino acids in starvation
  8. Protease inhibition – α₁-antitrypsin protects the lungs; its deficiency causes emphysema
  9. Acute-phase response – CRP, fibrinogen and haptoglobin rise in inflammation and infection

D. Clinical importance

  • Low albumin – oedema and ascites in cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition; more free (active) drug, so drug toxicity
  • Low clotting factors – bleeding in liver disease
  • Raised globulins and fibrinogen – raised ESR
  • Low immunoglobulins – repeated infections

E. Plasma and serum

  • Serum is plasma without fibrinogen and clotting factors (used up during clotting) – so protein tests are usually done on serum

F. Nursing points

  • Monitor daily weight, oedema, ascites and urine output in patients with low albumin
  • Give IV albumin slowly as prescribed and watch for fluid overload
  • Encourage a protein-rich diet in burns, surgery and malnutrition unless restricted
  • In patients with low albumin, watch for drug toxicity (e.g. phenytoin), as more free drug is present

Conclusion Plasma proteins – albumin, globulins and fibrinogen – maintain oncotic pressure, transport substances, defend the body, help clotting and buffer the blood; their levels help in diagnosing liver, kidney, nutritional and immune disorders.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the urea cycle and its significance.
answer_html:
Introduction Ammonia produced from amino acids is highly toxic, especially to the brain. The urea cycle (ornithine cycle, Krebs–Henseleit cycle) converts ammonia into urea, which is non-toxic, water-soluble and excreted by the kidneys.

A. Site – liver only; the first two steps are in the mitochondria and the rest in the cytosol

B. Sources and transport of ammonia

  • Deamination of amino acids, intestinal bacteria (absorbed into the portal blood), breakdown of purines and amines
  • Carried in blood mainly as glutamine (from tissues) and alanine (from muscle)

C. Steps

  1. NH₃ + CO₂ + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate – enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-I (rate-limiting; activated by N-acetylglutamate) – mitochondria
  2. Carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline – ornithine transcarbamoylase – mitochondria
  3. Citrulline moves to the cytosol; citrulline + aspartate + ATP → argininosuccinate – argininosuccinate synthetase
  4. Argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate – argininosuccinate lyase
  5. Arginine → urea + ornithine – arginase; ornithine returns to the mitochondria to repeat the cycle

D. Summary

  • One nitrogen comes from ammonia and the other from aspartate; carbon comes from CO₂
  • 3 ATP (four high-energy bonds) are used for each urea molecule
  • Fumarate links the urea cycle to the TCA cycle

E. Significance

  • Detoxification of ammonia
  • Main route of nitrogen excretion – urea forms about 80–90% of urinary nitrogen
  • Synthesis of arginine
  • Normal values – blood urea 15–40 mg/dl; urinary urea about 20–30 g/day (varies with protein intake)

F. Clinical significance

  • Hyperammonaemia – ammonia toxicity causes vomiting, irritability, confusion, flapping tremor, convulsions and coma
    • acquired – liver failure / cirrhosis (hepatic encephalopathy)
    • inherited – deficiency of urea cycle enzymes (ornithine transcarbamoylase deficiency is commonest) – presents in newborns
  • Blood urea – low in severe liver disease and low-protein diets; high in kidney failure, dehydration, GI bleeding and high-protein diets

G. Nursing points in hepatic encephalopathy

  • Monitor level of consciousness and flapping tremor
  • Give lactulose as prescribed (reduces ammonia absorption); prevent constipation
  • Avoid sedatives; watch for GI bleeding and infection, which raise ammonia
  • Protein intake as advised by the doctor/dietitian

Conclusion The urea cycle in the liver converts toxic ammonia to urea through carbamoyl phosphate, citrulline, argininosuccinate and arginine; its failure in liver disease or enzyme defects causes dangerous hyperammonaemia.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the biologically important compounds formed from amino acids.
answer_html:
Introduction Besides building proteins, amino acids are precursors of many vital compounds – hormones, neurotransmitters, pigments and other molecules.

A. Compounds formed from individual amino acids

Amino acid Important compounds formed
Glycine haem (with succinyl CoA), creatine, glutathione, purines, conjugated bile acids; an inhibitory neurotransmitter
Phenylalanine converted to tyrosine
Tyrosine dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline (catecholamines); thyroxine (T₄) and T₃; melanin
Tryptophan serotonin (5-HT), melatonin, niacin (vitamin B₃)
Histidine histamine
Glutamate GABA (inhibitory neurotransmitter), glutamine, glutathione
Arginine nitric oxide (vasodilator), creatine, urea
Methionine S-adenosylmethionine – the main methyl donor (for adrenaline, creatine, choline); cysteine
Cysteine glutathione, taurine (bile salts), part of coenzyme A
Aspartate purines, pyrimidines; enters the urea cycle
Serine sphingosine, phospholipids, ethanolamine, choline
Lysine + methionine carnitine (carries fatty acids into mitochondria)
Ornithine polyamines (spermine, spermidine) – cell growth

B. Functions of some of these compounds

  • Catecholamines – stress response, heart rate, BP; dopamine in movement control
  • Thyroid hormones – metabolic rate and growth
  • Serotonin – mood, sleep, gut movement; melatonin – sleep–wake cycle
  • Histamine – allergy, gastric acid secretion
  • Creatine phosphate – energy store in muscle; its breakdown product creatinine is a kidney function marker
  • Glutathione – protects red cells against oxidative damage
  • Nitric oxide – relaxes blood vessels; nitroglycerine for angina acts by releasing NO

C. Clinical aspects

  • Parkinson's disease – dopamine deficiency; treated with levodopa
  • Phenylketonuria – less tyrosine, so less melanin (light skin and hair)
  • Carcinoid tumour – tryptophan is diverted to serotonin, causing niacin deficiency (pellagra)
  • Antihistamines treat allergies; H₂ blockers reduce acid
  • Some antidepressants increase serotonin activity
  • Vitamin B₆ is needed for forming GABA, serotonin, dopamine and histamine – B₆ deficiency (e.g. during isoniazid therapy) can cause fits and neuropathy

D. Biogenic amines

  • Formed by decarboxylation of amino acids (needs vitamin B₆): histamine (histidine), serotonin (5-hydroxytryptophan), dopamine (DOPA), GABA (glutamate) and tyramine (tyrosine)
  • They act as neurotransmitters, hormones and local mediators

E. Nursing relevance

  • Levodopa is given with carbidopa; a high-protein meal can reduce its absorption – spread protein through the day
  • Patients on MAO-inhibitor antidepressants must avoid tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, fermented foods) – risk of a sudden rise of BP
  • Melatonin is used for sleep problems and jet lag

Conclusion Amino acids give rise to hormones (thyroxine, adrenaline), neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine, GABA), haem, creatine, glutathione, nitric oxide, niacin and melanin; their disorders explain diseases such as Parkinson's disease and pellagra.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the inborn errors of aromatic amino acid metabolism.

diagram.caption: Phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism with enzyme blocks

answer_html:
Introduction Inborn errors of metabolism are inherited disorders (mostly autosomal recessive) in which deficiency of one enzyme blocks a metabolic pathway. The substance before the block accumulates and the product after it is deficient. The aromatic amino acids are phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan.

1. Phenylketonuria (PKU)

  • Defect: phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin)
  • Accumulates: phenylalanine and phenylketones (phenylpyruvate) in blood and urine
  • Features: intellectual disability, seizures, light skin and hair, eczema, mousy odour
  • Diagnosis: newborn screening; ferric chloride test (green colour)
  • Treatment: low-phenylalanine diet from early infancy; tyrosine supplementation

2. Alkaptonuria

  • Defect: homogentisate oxidase
  • Accumulates: homogentisic acid, excreted in urine
  • Features:
    • urine turns black on standing (oxidation) – nappies stain dark
    • ochronosis – bluish-black pigment in cartilage, ears and sclera in adults
    • arthritis of large joints and spine in later life
  • Treatment: no cure; low-protein diet, vitamin C, pain relief; nitisinone in some cases

3. Albinism

  • Defect: tyrosinase in melanocytes – no melanin
  • Features: white hair, pale skin, light or pink eyes, photophobia, nystagmus, poor vision; high risk of sunburn and skin cancer
  • Care: protect from sunlight (clothing, hats, sunscreen), dark glasses, regular eye and skin checks

4. Tyrosinaemia

  • Type I (most severe) – defect of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase; liver failure, kidney tubule damage, rickets, cabbage-like odour; treated with nitisinone and diet
  • Type II – tyrosine aminotransferase defect; eye and skin lesions, intellectual disability

5. Hartnup disease (tryptophan)

  • Defect in intestinal and renal transport of neutral amino acids; tryptophan is lost, so niacin is deficient → pellagra-like skin rash, ataxia; treated with niacin and high-protein diet

Summary table

Disorder Enzyme defect Key feature
Phenylketonuria phenylalanine hydroxylase intellectual disability, mousy odour
Alkaptonuria homogentisate oxidase black urine, ochronosis, arthritis
Albinism tyrosinase absent melanin
Tyrosinaemia I fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase liver and kidney failure

6. Nursing role

  • Support newborn screening – heel-prick sample after 48 hours of feeding
  • Teach parents the special diet and regular blood monitoring
  • Genetic counselling – recurrence risk of 25% in each pregnancy for recessive disorders
  • Early detection prevents brain damage in PKU

Conclusion Phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria, albinism and tyrosinaemia result from single enzyme defects in phenylalanine–tyrosine metabolism; early detection by newborn screening and dietary management prevent many of their complications.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define electrophoresis. Explain its types and the normal serum protein pattern.

diagram.caption: Serum protein electrophoresis – normal and abnormal patterns

answer_html:
A. Definition Electrophoresis is the movement of charged particles (such as proteins) in an electric field. It is used to separate proteins according to their charge, size and shape.

B. Principle

  • At pH 8.6 (barbitone buffer), plasma proteins carry a negative charge and move towards the anode (+)
  • Albumin – most negative and smallest – moves fastest; gamma globulins move slowest

C. Types

  1. Moving boundary (free) electrophoresis – Tiselius; in solution; mainly of historical value
  2. Zone electrophoresis – on a supporting medium:
    • paper
    • cellulose acetate – common for serum proteins
    • agar/agarose gel – serum proteins, isoenzymes, DNA
    • starch gel
    • polyacrylamide gel (PAGE, SDS-PAGE) – separates by size
  3. Immunoelectrophoresis and immunofixation – identify specific immunoglobulins (myeloma)
  4. Isoelectric focusing – separates by isoelectric point
  5. Capillary electrophoresis – automated, used in modern laboratories (e.g. HbA1c, haemoglobin variants)
  6. Two-dimensional electrophoresis – research

D. Procedure in brief (serum proteins)

  • Apply serum near the cathode end of the strip → run in buffer at pH 8.6 → stain (e.g. amido black) → wash → measure bands by densitometry

E. Normal serum pattern – five bands (anode to cathode)

Band Approximate share Main proteins
Albumin 55–65% albumin
α₁-globulin 2–5% α₁-antitrypsin
α₂-globulin 7–13% haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin
β-globulin 8–14% transferrin, LDL, C3
γ-globulin 12–22% immunoglobulins

F. Abnormal patterns

  • Multiple myeloma – a sharp M band (spike) in the gamma region
  • Liver cirrhosis – low albumin, broad rise of gamma (beta–gamma bridging)
  • Nephrotic syndrome – very low albumin, raised α₂
  • Chronic infections – broad (polyclonal) rise in gamma
  • Acute inflammation – raised α₁ and α₂
  • Hypogammaglobulinaemia – small gamma band

G. Applications

  • Serum and urine protein electrophoresis (Bence Jones proteins)
  • Haemoglobin electrophoresis – sickle cell disease (HbS), thalassaemia trait (raised HbA₂)
  • Isoenzymes – CK and LDH
  • Lipoprotein patterns; DNA analysis (DNA fingerprinting)

H. Nursing responsibilities in sample collection

  • Serum protein electrophoresis – clotted blood in a plain tube; avoid haemolysis
  • Haemoglobin electrophoresis – blood in an EDTA tube; record any blood transfusion in the last 3 months, as donor blood alters the result
  • Urine protein electrophoresis – 24-hour or early-morning urine as ordered
  • Label correctly and send to the laboratory promptly
