Conclusion Electrophoresis separates charged proteins in an electric field; the normal serum pattern shows albumin and α₁, α₂, β and γ globulins, and changes in this pattern help diagnose myeloma, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome and haemoglobin disorders.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain microalbuminuria and the methods of detecting protein in urine.
answer_html:
Introduction A healthy person excretes less than 150 mg of protein and less than 30 mg of albumin in urine per day. Detection of urinary protein is a simple, important test for kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension and pre-eclampsia.

A. Qualitative (screening) tests

  1. Heat coagulation test
    • Fill a test tube two-thirds with clear urine and heat the upper part
    • Turbidity appears; add a few drops of 1% acetic acid
    • Turbidity that persists = protein; turbidity that clears = phosphates
  2. Sulphosalicylic acid test – add 20% sulphosalicylic acid; white turbidity = protein; detects all proteins including Bence Jones proteins
  3. Heller's nitric acid test – a white ring at the junction of urine and concentrated nitric acid
  4. Dipstick (reagent strip) – colour change of an indicator dye; quick bedside test graded trace to 4+; mainly detects albumin

B. Quantitative tests

  1. 24-hour urine protein
    • Normal: below 150 mg/day; nephrotic range: more than 3.5 g/day
  2. Spot urine protein–creatinine ratio (UPCR) – avoids a 24-hour collection
  3. Urine albumin–creatinine ratio (UACR) – the preferred test for early kidney damage

C. Microalbuminuria

  • Definition: urinary albumin of 30–300 mg/day (UACR 30–300 mg/g) – too little to be detected by a routine dipstick
  • Significance:
    • the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy – kidney damage can be slowed if detected now
    • marker of kidney damage in hypertension
    • indicates higher risk of heart disease
  • More than 300 mg/day = macroalbuminuria (overt proteinuria)
  • Diabetic patients should have UACR tested at least once a year

D. Collection of samples – nursing responsibilities

  • First morning midstream sample for routine tests; clean container
  • Avoid contamination with vaginal discharge or menstrual blood
  • 24-hour collection:
    • discard the first morning sample and note the time
    • collect all urine for the next 24 hours, including the sample at the same time next day
    • keep the container cool; label correctly; record intake–output
  • Test urine for protein at every antenatal visit (pre-eclampsia)

E. Bence Jones protein

  • Detected by heat test (precipitates at 40–60 °C, redissolves on boiling) and confirmed by urine electrophoresis

Conclusion Urinary protein is detected by heat coagulation, sulphosalicylic acid and dipstick tests and measured by 24-hour protein or UACR; microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day) is the earliest warning of diabetic kidney damage.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the six classes of enzymes with one example each.
answer_html:
Introduction Enzymes are biological catalysts – mostly proteins – that speed up chemical reactions in the body without being used up. The International Union of Biochemistry (IUBMB) groups them into six main classes (mnemonic "OTHLIL").

Class Reaction Example
1. Oxidoreductases oxidation–reduction lactate dehydrogenase
2. Transferases transfer of a group ALT, AST, hexokinase
3. Hydrolases breakdown by water amylase, lipase, pepsin
4. Lyases removal of a group without water, forming a double bond aldolase, fumarase
5. Isomerases rearrangement within a molecule triose phosphate isomerase
6. Ligases (synthetases) joining two molecules using ATP glutamine synthetase

Note: a seventh class, translocases (move molecules across membranes), was added in 2018.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What are coenzymes? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Coenzymes are non-protein organic molecules that combine with an enzyme protein (apoenzyme) to form the active enzyme (holoenzyme). They carry groups or electrons during the reaction.

  • Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + coenzyme
  • Metal ions that help enzymes (Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺) are called cofactors

Examples – most coenzymes come from B-complex vitamins

Coenzyme Vitamin Role
TPP thiamine (B₁) pyruvate dehydrogenase
FAD, FMN riboflavin (B₂) oxidation–reduction
NAD⁺, NADP⁺ niacin (B₃) dehydrogenases
Coenzyme A pantothenic acid (B₅) carries acyl groups
Pyridoxal phosphate pyridoxine (B₆) transaminases
Biotin biotin (B₇) carboxylation
Tetrahydrofolate folic acid one-carbon transfer

Significance: deficiency of a B-vitamin reduces the activity of enzymes that need it – e.g. thiamine deficiency (beriberi) impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase, causing lactic acidosis and nerve damage.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive enzyme inhibition.
answer_html:
Point Competitive inhibition Non-competitive inhibition
Inhibitor resembles the substrate does not resemble the substrate
Binding site the active site another site on the enzyme
Effect of more substrate inhibition is reversed not reversed
Km (affinity) increased unchanged
Vmax unchanged decreased
Drug examples statins (HMG CoA reductase), allopurinol (xanthine oxidase), methotrexate (dihydrofolate reductase), sulphonamides heavy metals (lead, mercury), cyanide (cytochrome oxidase)

Irreversible inhibition: the inhibitor binds permanently, e.g. organophosphate insecticides (acetylcholinesterase) and aspirin (cyclo-oxygenase).

Clinical uses of inhibition

  • Methanol poisoning is treated with ethanol or fomepizole, which compete for alcohol dehydrogenase and prevent formation of toxic formaldehyde
  • In organophosphate poisoning, pralidoxime reactivates the inhibited acetylcholinesterase if given early

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the therapeutic uses of enzymes.
answer_html:
Introduction Some enzymes are used as drugs for treatment.

Therapeutic enzymes

  1. Streptokinase, urokinase, alteplase (tPA), tenecteplase – dissolve clots (thrombolysis) in myocardial infarction, stroke and pulmonary embolism
  2. L-asparaginase – treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
  3. Hyaluronidase – increases spread and absorption of subcutaneous fluids (hypodermoclysis) and local anaesthetics
  4. Pancreatic enzymes (pancreatin, pancrelipase) – pancreatic insufficiency, cystic fibrosis
  5. Lactase – lactose intolerance
  6. Collagenase, papain, trypsin – debridement of wounds and burns
  7. Dornase alfa (DNase) – thins mucus in cystic fibrosis
  8. Enzyme replacement in rare storage diseases (e.g. Gaucher's disease)

Also used in diagnosis – glucose oxidase (glucometer strips), urease (blood urea), peroxidase in ELISA kits.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the enzymes raised in acute pancreatitis and their significance.
answer_html:
Enzymes raised

  1. Serum amylase
    • Rises within 2–12 hours of onset, peaks in about 24 hours and returns to normal in 3–5 days
    • A value more than 3 times the upper limit supports the diagnosis
    • Also raised in mumps, perforated peptic ulcer, intestinal obstruction, ruptured ectopic pregnancy and kidney failure – so it is less specific
  2. Serum lipase
    • More specific to the pancreas
    • Remains raised longer (7–14 days) – useful when the patient comes late
  3. Urinary amylase – stays raised for a longer time than serum amylase

Note: the level of the enzyme does not indicate how severe the pancreatitis is.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is the De Ritis ratio? Give its significance.
answer_html:
Definition The De Ritis ratio is the ratio of serum AST (SGOT) to ALT (SGPT).

Normal: about 0.8–1

Significance

  1. Less than 1 (ALT higher than AST) – acute viral hepatitis and most other acute liver cell injuries, because ALT is mainly a liver enzyme
  2. More than 2 (AST much higher) – alcoholic liver disease
    • alcohol damages mitochondria, which contain AST
    • alcoholics are often deficient in vitamin B₆, which lowers ALT activity
  3. More than 1 – cirrhosis and advanced liver disease
  4. AST also rises in heart and muscle injury, so the ratio must be read with the clinical picture

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Describe the diagnostic enzymes in liver disease.
answer_html:
Introduction Liver cells contain several enzymes that leak into blood when they are damaged or when bile flow is blocked. Measuring them helps to detect liver disease, tell its type and follow its course. (Normal ranges vary between laboratories.)

A. Enzymes of liver cell (hepatocellular) damage

1. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT/SGPT)

  • Normal: about 7–40 U/L
  • Found mainly in the cytoplasm of liver cells – the most specific marker of liver cell injury
  • Very high (often above 1,000 U/L) in acute viral hepatitis, drug or toxin injury (paracetamol overdose) and ischaemic hepatitis

2. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST/SGOT)

  • Normal: about 5–40 U/L
  • Present in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney and red cells – less specific
  • AST : ALT more than 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease

B. Enzymes of cholestasis (bile obstruction)

3. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)

  • Normal: about 40–130 U/L in adults
  • Lines the bile canaliculi; also present in bone, placenta and intestine
  • Markedly raised (more than 3 times) in obstructive jaundice (gallstones, carcinoma head of pancreas), intrahepatic cholestasis and liver metastases
  • Physiologically higher in growing children and pregnancy

4. Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)

  • Raised in cholestasis along with ALP – confirms that a high ALP comes from the liver and not bone
  • A sensitive marker of alcohol abuse; also raised by drugs such as phenytoin

5. 5′-Nucleotidase

  • Raised in cholestasis; like GGT, confirms the liver origin of ALP

C. Other enzymes

  • LDH (LDH₅ isoenzyme) – liver injury and liver metastases
  • Pseudocholinesterase – made by the liver; falls in liver disease (prolonged action of suxamethonium)

D. Patterns

Pattern ALT/AST ALP/GGT Example
Hepatocellular very high normal or mildly raised viral hepatitis
Cholestatic mildly raised very high gallstone in common bile duct
Alcoholic AST > 2 × ALT GGT high alcoholic hepatitis

E. Note

  • Enzymes show damage, not liver function; albumin and prothrombin time show the liver's synthetic function

F. Nursing points

  • Avoid haemolysis of the sample (red cells contain AST and LDH)
  • Record history of alcohol and drugs; monitor serial values to judge recovery
  • Explain that enzyme levels fall as the liver heals

Conclusion ALT and AST indicate liver cell injury, while ALP, GGT and 5′-nucleotidase indicate cholestasis; their pattern helps to distinguish hepatitis, obstructive jaundice and alcoholic liver disease.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the enzymes and cardiac markers used in the diagnosis of myocardial infarction.

diagram.caption: Rise and fall of cardiac markers after myocardial infarction
labels: hours and days after chest pain

answer_html:
Introduction In myocardial infarction (MI), dead heart muscle cells release proteins and enzymes into blood. These cardiac markers confirm the diagnosis together with the history and ECG. Their time of rise and fall is important.

A. Cardiac troponins (cTnI and cTnT) – the preferred markers

  • Proteins of heart muscle, highly specific and sensitive
  • Rise in 3–4 hours (high-sensitivity tests detect them within 1–3 hours), peak at 12–24 hours
  • Remain raised for 7–14 days – useful for patients who come late
  • A rise above the laboratory's upper reference limit with a rising or falling trend indicates MI

B. Creatine kinase – MB isoenzyme (CK-MB)

  • Rises in 4–6 hours, peaks at 18–24 hours, returns to normal in 2–3 days
  • Because it falls early, it is useful to detect re-infarction

C. Total creatine kinase (CK)

  • Rises in 4–6 hours, peaks at 24 hours, normal in 3–4 days
  • Also raised by skeletal muscle injury – IM injections, exercise, surgery – so not specific

D. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)

  • Rises in 12–24 hours, peaks at 2–3 days, remains raised 10–14 days
  • In MI, LDH₁ becomes higher than LDH₂ ("flipped" pattern)
  • Now rarely used

E. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)

  • Rises in 6–8 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours, normal in 4–6 days
  • Not specific (liver, muscle) – no longer used for MI

F. Myoglobin

  • Earliest marker – rises in 1–3 hours; normal within 24 hours
  • Not specific (skeletal muscle); a normal value helps rule out MI early

Summary table

Marker Rises Peaks Returns to normal
Myoglobin 1–3 h 6–12 h 24 h
Troponin 3–4 h 12–24 h 7–14 days
CK-MB 4–6 h 18–24 h 2–3 days
AST 6–8 h 24–48 h 4–6 days
LDH 12–24 h 2–3 days 10–14 days

G. Nursing responsibilities

  • Note the exact time of onset of chest pain
  • Collect serial samples (on arrival and repeated after a few hours as ordered); label with time
  • Record an ECG immediately; report results urgently
  • Avoid IM injections in suspected MI (they raise CK and are risky if thrombolysis is given)

Conclusion Troponins are the most specific markers of MI and remain raised for up to two weeks, CK-MB helps detect re-infarction, and older enzymes such as LDH and AST are now of limited value; markers are always interpreted with the ECG and symptoms.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the diagnostic applications of enzymes.
answer_html:
Introduction Clinical enzymology is the measurement of enzymes in blood and body fluids to diagnose disease, judge its severity and monitor treatment. Enzymes are useful because many are specific to particular organs.

A. Types of plasma enzymes

  1. Functional plasma enzymes
    • Secreted into plasma, where they act
    • e.g. clotting factors (prothrombin), lipoprotein lipase, pseudocholinesterase, ceruloplasmin
    • Mostly made by the liver – their levels fall in liver disease
  2. Non-functional plasma enzymes
    • Act inside cells; normally present in plasma in small amounts
    • e.g. ALT, AST, CK, LDH, ALP, amylase, lipase, acid phosphatase
    • Their levels rise when cells are damaged – the basis of diagnostic enzymology

B. Reasons for raised plasma enzymes

  • Cell damage or death (MI, hepatitis)
  • Increased cell activity or turnover (ALP in bone growth)
  • Increased enzyme production (GGT in alcohol use)
  • Obstruction to normal excretion (ALP in obstructive jaundice)
  • Reduced clearance (amylase in kidney failure)

C. Organ-wise diagnostic enzymes

Organ / condition Enzymes
Heart (MI) troponin (marker), CK-MB, LDH₁
Liver ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, 5′-nucleotidase
Pancreas amylase, lipase
Skeletal muscle CK (CK-MM), aldolase
Bone ALP (bone isoenzyme)
Prostate PSA, acid phosphatase
Tuberculous effusions adenosine deaminase (ADA) in pleural or peritoneal fluid
Red cells G6PD – deficiency causes haemolysis with some drugs (primaquine, dapsone)
Organophosphate poisoning low cholinesterase activity

D. Enzymes as laboratory reagents

  • Glucose oxidase–peroxidase – blood glucose and glucometer strips
  • Urease – blood urea; cholesterol oxidase – cholesterol
  • Horseradish peroxidase and ALP in ELISA kits; Taq polymerase in PCR

E. Precautions in enzyme testing

  • Avoid haemolysis – red cells contain LDH, AST and acid phosphatase
  • Separate serum promptly; do not heat or freeze unless instructed
  • Note recent IM injections, exercise and drugs
  • Use the laboratory's own reference ranges

F. Advantages and limitations

  • Advantages – simple blood tests, early diagnosis, help in judging severity and monitoring recovery (falling values)
  • Limitations – few enzymes are absolutely organ-specific; levels are affected by haemolysis, exercise, IM injections, drugs and age; results must be read with the clinical picture and other tests
  • Isoenzyme measurement improves specificity

Conclusion Diagnostic enzymology is based on non-functional plasma enzymes that rise when specific organs are damaged; organ-wise enzyme patterns, along with enzyme reagents used in routine tests, make enzymes valuable tools in diagnosis.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define isoenzymes. Explain their properties and clinical importance.
answer_html:
A. Definition Isoenzymes (isozymes) are different molecular forms of the same enzyme that catalyse the same reaction but differ in their structure, physical, chemical and immunological properties. They are coded by different genes and are distributed differently in tissues.

B. Properties

  1. Catalyse the same chemical reaction
  2. Differ in amino acid composition or subunit make-up
  3. Differ in electrophoretic mobility – so they can be separated by electrophoresis
  4. Differ in heat stability – e.g. bone ALP is destroyed by heat; placental ALP is heat-stable
  5. Differ in sensitivity to inhibitors – e.g. prostatic acid phosphatase is inhibited by tartrate
  6. Differ in affinity for substrate (Km) and in reaction with antibodies
  7. Have characteristic tissue distribution – the key to their diagnostic use

C. Important examples

1. Creatine kinase (CK) – dimer of M and B subunits

  • CK-1 (BB) – brain
  • CK-2 (MB) – heart – marker of MI
  • CK-3 (MM) – skeletal muscle (and heart)

2. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) – tetramer of H and M subunits; five isoenzymes

  • LDH₁ (H₄) and LDH₂ – heart, red cells, kidney
  • LDH₃ – lungs, lymphoid tissue
  • LDH₄ and LDH₅ (M₄) – liver and skeletal muscle
  • Normally LDH₂ > LDH₁; in MI, LDH₁ > LDH₂ ("flipped pattern")

3. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)

  • Liver, bone, placental, intestinal forms
  • Regan isoenzyme (placental-like) appears in some cancers

4. Others

  • Acid phosphatase – prostatic and red-cell forms
  • Amylase – pancreatic and salivary forms

D. Clinical importance

  • Identify the organ of origin of a raised enzyme:
    • CK-MB – heart; CK-MM – skeletal muscle
    • LDH₅ – liver; LDH₁ – heart, haemolysis
    • bone ALP versus liver ALP
  • Diagnosis of MI (CK-MB), liver disease and bone disease
  • Tumour markers – Regan isoenzyme, prostatic acid phosphatase
  • Distinguish pancreatitis (pancreatic amylase) from mumps (salivary amylase)

E. Methods of separation

  • Electrophoresis, heat inactivation, inhibitors, immunological methods

F. Nursing relevance

  • Haemolysed samples falsely raise LDH₁ – draw blood gently with an adequate needle size and mix tubes gently
  • IM injections and strenuous exercise raise CK-MM – note them on the request form
  • Send samples at the times ordered, as isoenzyme patterns change with time after injury

Conclusion Isoenzymes are different forms of an enzyme with the same action but different structure and tissue distribution; measuring them – especially CK, LDH and ALP isoenzymes – shows which organ is damaged.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the diagnostic enzymes in muscle disease, bone disease and prostate cancer.
answer_html:
Introduction Specific enzymes help in the diagnosis of diseases of skeletal muscle, bone and the prostate.

A. Muscle disease

1. Creatine kinase (CK) – mainly CK-MM

  • The most sensitive marker of muscle damage
  • Very high in:
    • Duchenne muscular dystrophy – raised even before symptoms; also helps detect female carriers
    • polymyositis and dermatomyositis
    • rhabdomyolysis – crush injury, heat stroke, severe exercise, statin-induced myopathy
  • Mild rise after IM injections, exercise, surgery
  • Normal in nerve-origin weakness (myasthenia gravis, poliomyelitis) – helps to distinguish muscle from nerve disease

2. Aldolase

  • Raised in muscular dystrophy and polymyositis

3. Others – AST, LDH and myoglobin (myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis can damage the kidneys)

B. Bone disease

1. Alkaline phosphatase (bone ALP) – produced by osteoblasts (bone-forming cells)

  • Normal adult ALP about 40–130 U/L; higher in growing children
  • Raised in:
    • Paget's disease of bone – very high
    • rickets and osteomalacia
    • bone secondaries (especially from prostate cancer), osteosarcoma
    • hyperparathyroidism, healing fractures
  • Usually normal in osteoporosis

2. Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) – reflects bone breakdown by osteoclasts

C. Prostate cancer

1. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)

  • A protease enzyme made by prostate epithelium
  • Normal: usually below 4 ng/ml (increases with age); 4–10 ng/ml – grey zone; above 10 ng/ml – cancer likely
  • Also raised in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, after catheterisation or rectal examination
  • Low free-to-total PSA ratio favours cancer
  • Uses – screening, diagnosis and follow-up after surgery or radiotherapy (a rising PSA indicates recurrence)

2. Prostatic acid phosphatase (ACP)

  • Inhibited by tartrate; raised in metastatic prostate cancer
  • Largely replaced by PSA

D. Nursing responsibilities

  • Avoid IM injections and strenuous exercise before CK testing
  • Collect PSA before rectal examination or catheterisation (or wait a few days)
  • Avoid haemolysis for acid phosphatase
  • Explain to patients that one abnormal value needs repeat and further tests

E. Summary table

Condition Main enzyme Remark
Muscular dystrophy, myositis, rhabdomyolysis CK (CK-MM), aldolase very high in Duchenne dystrophy
Paget's disease, rickets, osteomalacia, bone secondaries ALP (bone) normal in osteoporosis
Prostate cancer PSA, prostatic ACP PSA used for screening and follow-up

Conclusion CK and aldolase indicate muscle damage, alkaline phosphatase indicates increased bone formation, and PSA (with acid phosphatase) is used to detect and monitor prostate cancer.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the factors affecting enzyme activity.

diagram.caption: Effect of substrate concentration, temperature and pH on enzyme activity

answer_html:
Introduction Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up reactions by binding the substrate at their active site. Their activity depends on several factors.

1. Substrate concentration

  • At low substrate levels, the rate rises steeply as substrate increases
  • At high levels all enzyme molecules are busy (saturated) – the rate reaches a maximum (Vmax)
  • Km (Michaelis constant) – the substrate concentration at half of Vmax; a low Km means high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate
  • The graph is a hyperbola

2. Enzyme concentration

  • When substrate is plentiful, the rate is directly proportional to the amount of enzyme

3. Temperature

  • Activity rises with temperature up to the optimum temperature (about 37 °C for human enzymes)
  • Above this, the enzyme is denatured and activity falls sharply (above about 50–60 °C)
  • Low temperature slows activity without destroying the enzyme – the reason samples and vaccines are refrigerated, and why therapeutic hypothermia reduces tissue metabolism

4. pH

  • Each enzyme has an optimum pH:
    • pepsin about 2
    • salivary amylase about 6.8
    • trypsin about 8
    • alkaline phosphatase about 10; acid phosphatase about 5
  • Extremes of pH change the charge of the active site or denature the enzyme

5. Concentration of products

  • Accumulating products slow the reaction; end products may inhibit key enzymes (feedback inhibition)

6. Activators

  • Metal ions – Mg²⁺ (kinases), Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺; chloride activates salivary amylase
  • Coenzymes derived from B-vitamins

7. Inhibitors

  • Competitive (statins, allopurinol), non-competitive (heavy metals) and irreversible (organophosphates) inhibitors reduce activity

8. Time

  • Enzymes lose activity over time; products accumulate

9. Radiation

  • UV light and X-rays denature enzymes

10. Regulation in the body

  • Allosteric regulation, phosphorylation (switched on and off by hormones), and induction or repression of enzyme synthesis (alcohol and phenytoin induce liver enzymes)

Clinical relevance

  • High fever increases metabolism and oxygen need; very high fever can denature enzymes
  • Many drugs act by inhibiting enzymes
  • Enzyme test samples must be stored and transported correctly

Nursing relevance

  • Keep enzyme test samples cool and deliver promptly; do not leave them in the sun or near heaters
  • In hypothermia, metabolism and drug breakdown slow down – drugs may act longer
  • Fever raises oxygen and calorie needs – increase fluids and nutrition

Conclusion Enzyme activity depends on substrate and enzyme concentration, temperature, pH, products, activators and inhibitors; these principles explain drug action, effects of fever and the correct handling of laboratory samples.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Differentiate between metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis.
answer_html:
Point Metabolic acidosis Metabolic alkalosis
Primary change fall in bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ below 22 mEq/L) rise in bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ above 26 mEq/L)
Blood pH below 7.35 above 7.45
Compensation hyperventilation – PaCO₂ falls hypoventilation – PaCO₂ rises
Common causes diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure, severe diarrhoea, methanol or aspirin poisoning persistent vomiting, nasogastric suction, diuretics, hypokalaemia, excess antacids or bicarbonate
Breathing deep, rapid (Kussmaul) slow, shallow
Other features confusion, low BP, arrhythmia, hyperkalaemia tetany, tingling, muscle cramps, hypokalaemia
Treatment treat cause; IV bicarbonate in severe cases treat cause; IV normal saline and potassium

Remember: in metabolic disorders, pH and HCO₃⁻ move in the same direction, and the lungs compensate by changing PaCO₂.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Write the normal values of arterial blood gas (ABG).
answer_html:
Introduction Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis measures the pH and gases of arterial blood. It shows the patient's acid–base status, ventilation and oxygenation.

Normal values

Parameter Normal value
pH 7.35–7.45
PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg
HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) 22–26 mEq/L
PaO₂ 80–100 mmHg (room air)
SaO₂ (oxygen saturation) 95–100%
Base excess –2 to +2 mEq/L

Remember

  • PaCO₂ is the respiratory component; HCO₃⁻ is the metabolic component
  • PaO₂ is lower in the elderly and higher in patients on oxygen

Uses of ABG

  • Diagnosis of acid–base disorders (acidosis, alkalosis) and their compensation
  • Assessment of respiratory failure and the need for oxygen or ventilation
  • Monitoring of patients on mechanical ventilation, in DKA, shock and poisoning

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the acids produced in the body.
answer_html:
Introduction Normal metabolism continuously produces acids, which the body must buffer and excrete to keep blood pH at 7.35–7.45.

1. Volatile acid

  • Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) – formed from the CO₂ of cellular respiration (about 15,000–20,000 mmol of CO₂ per day)
  • Excreted by the lungs as CO₂

2. Fixed (non-volatile) acids – about 50–100 mEq per day, excreted by the kidneys

  • Sulphuric acid – from sulphur-containing amino acids (methionine, cysteine)
  • Phosphoric acid – from phosphoproteins, phospholipids, nucleic acids
  • Lactic acid – anaerobic glycolysis (exercise, hypoxia)
  • Ketone bodies (acetoacetic and β-hydroxybutyric acids) – fasting, diabetes
  • Uric acid – from purines
  • Hydrochloric acid – from basic amino acids (lysine, arginine)

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define pH. Give the normal pH of blood.
answer_html:
Definition pH is the negative logarithm (to base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = –log [H⁺].

  • The scale runs from 0 to 14; 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline
  • A fall of one pH unit means a ten-fold rise in H⁺ concentration

Normal pH of blood

  • Arterial blood: 7.35–7.45 (average 7.4) – slightly alkaline
  • Venous blood is slightly lower (about 7.32–7.42), as it carries more CO₂

Abnormal values

  • Below 7.35 – acidaemia; above 7.45 – alkalaemia
  • Values below about 6.8 or above about 7.8 are usually not compatible with life

Why it matters: enzymes, heart rhythm, nerve function and oxygen delivery all depend on a stable pH.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is the anion gap? Give its normal value and significance.
answer_html:
Definition The anion gap is the difference between the measured cations and measured anions in serum:

  • Anion gap = Na⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)
  • Normal: about 8–16 mEq/L (12 ± 4)
  • It represents unmeasured anions – albumin, phosphate, sulphate and organic acids

Significance – type of metabolic acidosis

  1. High anion gap acidosis – an extra acid is added (mnemonic MUDPILES):
    • Methanol, Uraemia (kidney failure), Diabetic ketoacidosis, Paraldehyde, Isoniazid/iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylate (aspirin) poisoning
  2. Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis – bicarbonate is lost
    • diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, excess normal saline
  3. Low anion gap – low albumin, multiple myeloma

Example: Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 100, HCO₃⁻ 10 → anion gap = 140 – 110 = 30 mEq/L (high) – as in diabetic ketoacidosis.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation? State its significance.
answer_html:
Equation (bicarbonate buffer) pH = pKa + log ( [HCO₃⁻] ÷ [H₂CO₃] )

  • pKa of carbonic acid = 6.1
  • Normal HCO₃⁻ = 24 mEq/L; H₂CO₃ = 0.03 × PaCO₂ (40) = 1.2 mEq/L
  • Ratio 24 : 1.2 = 20 : 1; log 20 = 1.3
  • pH = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4

Significance

  1. Shows that blood pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid, not their absolute amounts
  2. As long as the 20 : 1 ratio is kept, pH stays normal – the basis of compensation
  3. HCO₃⁻ is controlled by the kidneys (metabolic part) and H₂CO₃/CO₂ by the lungs (respiratory part)
  4. Used to calculate HCO₃⁻ in ABG analysers

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the regulation of blood pH.

diagram.caption: Three lines of defence in regulation of blood pH
labels: kidneys – H+ excretion and HCO3 reabsorption (hours to days)

answer_html:
Introduction The normal pH of blood is 7.35–7.45. Although the body constantly produces acids, the pH is kept almost constant by three lines of defence: buffers, the lungs and the kidneys.

A. First line – chemical buffers (act within seconds) A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt that resists change in pH when an acid or alkali is added.

  1. Bicarbonate–carbonic acid buffer (HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃)
    • The most important buffer of extracellular fluid
    • Strong acids are converted to the weak carbonic acid → CO₂ is breathed out
    • Normal ratio 20 : 1
  2. Phosphate buffer (HPO₄²⁻/H₂PO₄⁻)
    • Important inside cells and in urine
  3. Protein buffers
    • Plasma proteins and intracellular proteins – the largest buffer capacity of the body
  4. Haemoglobin buffer
    • The main buffer for carbonic acid inside red cells
    • Chloride shift – bicarbonate formed in red cells moves into plasma in exchange for chloride

B. Second line – respiratory regulation (acts within minutes)

  • The respiratory centre responds to rising H⁺ and CO₂
  • Acidosis → faster, deeper breathing → more CO₂ removed → pH rises
  • Alkalosis → slower breathing → CO₂ retained → pH falls
  • Can correct only about 50–75% of a change; cannot remove fixed acids

C. Third line – renal regulation (hours to days; most powerful)

  1. Reabsorption of bicarbonate – almost all filtered HCO₃⁻ is reclaimed in the proximal tubule
  2. Excretion of H⁺ as titratable acid – combined with phosphate in urine
  3. Excretion of H⁺ as ammonium (NH₄⁺) – kidneys make ammonia from glutamine; very important in chronic acidosis
  4. Generation of new bicarbonate to replace what was used in buffering - Urine pH can vary from 4.5 to 8, showing the kidney's capacity

D. Comparison

Mechanism Speed Remark
Buffers seconds temporary; do not remove acid
Lungs minutes removes CO₂ (volatile acid)
Kidneys hours–days removes fixed acids; complete correction

E. Clinical relevance

  • Lung disease (COPD) → CO₂ retention → respiratory acidosis
  • Kidney failure → fixed acids retained → metabolic acidosis
  • Kussmaul breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis is respiratory compensation

Conclusion Blood pH is regulated by buffers (bicarbonate, phosphate, protein and haemoglobin) within seconds, by the lungs through CO₂ removal within minutes, and by the kidneys through H⁺ excretion and bicarbonate reabsorption over hours to days.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Describe the types of acid–base disorders with their causes and compensation.
answer_html:
Introduction Acid–base disorders are disturbances of blood pH. Acidosis is a process that lowers pH (below 7.35) and alkalosis a process that raises it (above 7.45). They are respiratory (primary change in PaCO₂) or metabolic (primary change in HCO₃⁻).

1. Respiratory acidosis

  • Definition: pH below 7.35 due to CO₂ retention (PaCO₂ above 45 mmHg) from inadequate breathing
  • Causes:
    • COPD, severe asthma, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema
    • depression of the respiratory centre – opioid or sedative overdose, head injury, anaesthesia
    • neuromuscular weakness – Guillain–Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, chest wall injury
    • airway obstruction
  • Compensation: kidneys retain bicarbonate (over 2–3 days)

2. Respiratory alkalosis

  • Definition: pH above 7.45 due to excess loss of CO₂ (PaCO₂ below 35 mmHg) from hyperventilation
  • Causes: anxiety and panic attacks, pain, fever, high altitude, early asthma, pulmonary embolism, salicylate poisoning (early), excessive mechanical ventilation, pregnancy, liver failure
  • Compensation: kidneys excrete bicarbonate

3. Metabolic acidosis

  • Definition: pH below 7.35 due to fall in HCO₃⁻ (below 22 mEq/L) – acid gain or bicarbonate loss
  • Causes:
    • acid gain – diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis (shock, hypoxia), kidney failure, methanol and salicylate poisoning
    • bicarbonate loss – severe diarrhoea, intestinal fistula, renal tubular acidosis
  • Compensation: hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) lowers PaCO₂

4. Metabolic alkalosis

  • Definition: pH above 7.45 due to rise in HCO₃⁻ (above 26 mEq/L) – acid loss or alkali gain
  • Causes: persistent vomiting and nasogastric aspiration (loss of HCl), diuretics, hypokalaemia, excess antacid or bicarbonate, Cushing's syndrome, hyperaldosteronism
  • Compensation: hypoventilation raises PaCO₂

Summary table

Disorder pH Primary change Compensation
Respiratory acidosis ↓ PaCO₂ ↑ HCO₃⁻ ↑
Respiratory alkalosis ↑ PaCO₂ ↓ HCO₃⁻ ↓
Metabolic acidosis ↓ HCO₃⁻ ↓ PaCO₂ ↓
Metabolic alkalosis ↑ HCO₃⁻ ↑ PaCO₂ ↑

5. Degrees of compensation

  • Uncompensated – pH abnormal; the other value normal
  • Partially compensated – pH abnormal; both values abnormal
  • Fully compensated – pH normal (towards the side of the primary disorder); both values abnormal
  • Mixed disorders – two primary disorders together (e.g. cardiac arrest: respiratory + metabolic acidosis)

6. Nursing points

  • Assess breathing pattern, level of consciousness, potassium, intake–output
  • Respiratory acidosis – airway care, positioning, controlled oxygen, avoid sedatives
  • Respiratory alkalosis – calm the patient, slow breathing
  • Monitor ABG and electrolytes as ordered

Conclusion The four primary acid–base disorders are respiratory acidosis and alkalosis (PaCO₂ changes) and metabolic acidosis and alkalosis (HCO₃⁻ changes); the lungs and kidneys compensate for each other to restore the 20 : 1 ratio.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the steps in interpreting an ABG report, with examples. Add the nurse's responsibilities in ABG sampling.
answer_html:
Introduction Arterial blood gas (ABG) interpretation helps identify acid–base disorders and oxygenation problems quickly. Nurses in ICUs and emergency units must read ABG reports and collect samples correctly.

A. Normal values (reference)

  • pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg; HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L; PaO₂ 80–100 mmHg; SaO₂ 95–100%

B. Steps of interpretation

  1. Look at the pH – below 7.35 acidaemia; above 7.45 alkalaemia
  2. Look at PaCO₂ – high = respiratory acidosis; low = respiratory alkalosis
  3. Look at HCO₃⁻ – low = metabolic acidosis; high = metabolic alkalosis
  4. Find the primary disorder – the value that matches the pH change
    • ROME: Respiratory – pH and PaCO₂ move Opposite; Metabolic – pH and HCO₃⁻ move Equal (same direction)
  5. Check compensation – uncompensated, partially or fully compensated
  6. Assess oxygenation – PaO₂ and SaO₂ (hypoxaemia if PaO₂ below 80 mmHg)
  7. In metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap
  8. Correlate with the patient's condition

C. Examples

pH PaCO₂ HCO₃⁻ Interpretation Likely situation
7.25 60 25 uncompensated respiratory acidosis opioid overdose, acute asthma
7.32 58 30 partially compensated respiratory acidosis COPD
7.28 28 13 metabolic acidosis, partially compensated diabetic ketoacidosis
7.50 48 34 metabolic alkalosis, partially compensated repeated vomiting
7.52 28 23 uncompensated respiratory alkalosis anxiety, hyperventilation

D. Nurse's responsibilities in ABG sampling

  1. Before
    • Explain the procedure; check anticoagulant therapy and platelet count
    • Perform the modified Allen's test before radial puncture to confirm ulnar collateral circulation
    • Note oxygen therapy (FiO₂) and body temperature; wait about 20–30 minutes after changing oxygen settings
  2. During
    • Use a pre-heparinised ABG syringe; aseptic technique
    • Common site – radial artery; others – brachial, femoral
    • Arterial blood fills the syringe by its own pressure (bright red, pulsatile)
  3. After
    • Apply firm pressure for at least 5 minutes (10 minutes or more if on anticoagulants)
    • Expel air bubbles, cap the syringe and mix gently
    • Send immediately – analyse within about 15–30 minutes, or as per laboratory guidance
    • Check the site and circulation of the hand; document

Conclusion ABG reports are read systematically – pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, primary disorder, compensation and oxygenation; correct sampling with Allen's test, heparinised syringe, no air bubbles and prompt analysis ensures reliable results.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Outline the pathway of haem degradation.
answer_html:
Introduction Old red cells (life span 120 days) are destroyed in the reticuloendothelial system (spleen, liver, bone marrow). Haemoglobin is split into globin (reused as amino acids) and haem.

Pathway

  1. Haem → biliverdin (green) – enzyme haem oxygenase; iron is released (stored and reused) and CO is formed
  2. Biliverdin → bilirubin (yellow, unconjugated) – biliverdin reductase
  3. Unconjugated bilirubin is carried in blood bound to albumin to the liver
  4. In the liver it is conjugated with glucuronic acid (UDP-glucuronyl transferase) → conjugated bilirubin (water-soluble)
  5. Excreted in bile → intestine → bacteria convert it to urobilinogen
  6. Most urobilinogen → stercobilin (brown colour of faeces); a little is reabsorbed and excreted in urine as urobilin

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is physiological jaundice of the newborn?
answer_html:
Definition Physiological jaundice is a mild, harmless unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia seen in many normal newborns.

Timing

  • Appears after 24 hours (day 2–3), peaks on day 3–5 and disappears by day 7–10 in term babies (up to 14 days in preterm)
  • Serum bilirubin usually stays below about 12–15 mg/dl in term babies

Causes

  1. High red-cell mass and shorter red-cell life (70–90 days) → more bilirubin
  2. Immature liver – low UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity
  3. Increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin; few gut bacteria

Management

  • Frequent breastfeeding (8–12 times a day); observe the colour of skin and eyes in daylight
  • Measure bilirubin if jaundice spreads to the palms and soles; phototherapy if levels exceed age-specific limits

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is the van den Bergh reaction? Give its significance.
answer_html:
Principle Bilirubin reacts with diazotised sulphanilic acid (Ehrlich's diazo reagent) to form a purple (reddish-violet) azobilirubin.

Types of reaction

  1. Direct reaction – colour appears immediately, without alcohol → conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin
  2. Indirect reaction – colour appears only after adding alcohol (methanol) → unconjugated bilirubin
  3. Biphasic reaction – partly immediate and partly after alcohol → both types increased

Significance

  • Direct positive – obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice
  • Indirect positive – haemolytic (pre-hepatic) jaundice
  • Biphasic – hepatocellular (hepatic) jaundice
  • Basis of the laboratory measurement of direct and indirect (total minus direct) bilirubin

Practical points: the sample should be fresh and protected from light (bilirubin breaks down in light) and free from haemolysis.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is kernicterus?
answer_html:
Definition Kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) is brain damage in newborns caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brain stem.

Why it occurs

  • Unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble; when its level exceeds the albumin-binding capacity, free bilirubin crosses the blood–brain barrier
  • Risk factors: prematurity, very high bilirubin (Rh/ABO haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency), hypoxia, acidosis, sepsis, hypothermia, low albumin, drugs that displace bilirubin (sulphonamides)

Features

  • Early – lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia, high-pitched cry
  • Later – opisthotonos, fits, fever

Sequelae – athetoid cerebral palsy, deafness, upward gaze palsy, intellectual disability

Prevention – early detection of jaundice, phototherapy and exchange transfusion when indicated.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Differentiate between conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin.
answer_html:
Point Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin Conjugated (direct) bilirubin
Formed in reticuloendothelial cells, from haem liver, by adding glucuronic acid
Solubility fat-soluble, water-insoluble water-soluble
Transport in blood bound to albumin mostly free
Van den Bergh reaction indirect (needs alcohol) direct (immediate)
Excreted in urine no yes (when raised)
Crosses blood–brain barrier yes – kernicterus in newborns no
Normal serum level 0.2–0.8 mg/dl 0–0.3 mg/dl
Raised in haemolysis, physiological jaundice, Gilbert's syndrome obstructive jaundice, hepatitis

Total serum bilirubin: normal 0.2–1.2 mg/dl; jaundice is visible when it exceeds about 2–2.5 mg/dl.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is urobilinogen? Give its significance.
answer_html:
Definition Urobilinogen is a colourless compound formed from conjugated bilirubin by intestinal bacteria.

Fate

  • Most is oxidised to stercobilin, which gives faeces their brown colour
  • About 10–20% is reabsorbed into the portal blood; most is re-excreted by the liver and a small amount appears in urine (normally 1–4 mg/day), where it is oxidised to urobilin (yellow)

Detection: Ehrlich's aldehyde test (pink-red colour) or urine dipstick.

Significance

Condition Urine urobilinogen
Haemolytic jaundice increased
Hepatocellular jaundice increased early (liver cannot re-excrete it); may fall later
Obstructive jaundice absent – bilirubin cannot reach the intestine
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce gut bacteria and therefore urobilinogen

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Describe the catabolism of haem – formation, transport, conjugation and excretion of bilirubin.

diagram.caption: Catabolism of haem and bilirubin metabolism

answer_html:
Introduction Haem is the iron-containing pigment of haemoglobin, myoglobin and cytochromes. About 80% of bilirubin comes from the haemoglobin of old red cells; the rest from other haem proteins and ineffective red-cell formation. An adult produces about 250–350 mg of bilirubin a day.

A. Breakdown of haemoglobin

  • Red cells live about 120 days; old cells are engulfed by macrophages of the spleen, liver and bone marrow
  • Haemoglobin → globin (broken down to amino acids, reused) + haem

B. Formation of bilirubin

  1. Haem → biliverdin – microsomal haem oxygenase; uses oxygen and NADPH
    • iron is released → stored as ferritin or carried by transferrin to the marrow for reuse
    • carbon monoxide (CO) is formed and exhaled
  2. Biliverdin (green) → bilirubin (orange-yellow) – biliverdin reductase - This is why a bruise changes colour from blue to green to yellow

C. Transport

  • Bilirubin is unconjugated, insoluble in water and toxic in the free form
  • It is carried in plasma tightly bound to albumin
  • Drugs such as sulphonamides and salicylates displace it from albumin

D. Uptake and conjugation in the liver

  1. Uptake – liver cells take up bilirubin (carrier-mediated) and bind it to the protein ligandin
  2. Conjugation – in the endoplasmic reticulum, the enzyme UDP-glucuronyl transferase adds two molecules of glucuronic acid → bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated bilirubin), which is water-soluble
  3. Secretion – conjugated bilirubin is actively secreted into bile canaliculi – the rate-limiting step

E. Fate in the intestine

  • Bacteria in the ileum and colon remove the glucuronic acid and reduce bilirubin to urobilinogen
  • Most urobilinogen → stercobilinogen → stercobilin – brown colour of stool
  • About 10–20% is reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation); most is re-excreted in bile and a small amount is excreted in urine as urobilinogen/urobilin (yellow colour of urine)

F. Normal values

  • Total serum bilirubin 0.2–1.2 mg/dl; direct 0–0.3 mg/dl
  • Urine: no bilirubin; urobilinogen present in traces

G. Disorders

  • Increased formation – haemolysis → haemolytic jaundice
  • Defective conjugation – neonatal (physiological) jaundice, Gilbert's syndrome (mild), Crigler–Najjar syndrome (severe)
  • Defective excretion – hepatitis, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor syndromes
  • Obstruction of bile flow – gallstones, carcinoma head of pancreas → obstructive jaundice

Conclusion Haem is converted to biliverdin and bilirubin in macrophages, carried by albumin to the liver, conjugated with glucuronic acid, excreted in bile and converted to urobilinogen and stercobilin; a defect at any step causes jaundice.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the types of jaundice with their causes and biochemical findings in blood and urine.
answer_html:
Introduction Jaundice (icterus) is the yellow colour of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes due to raised serum bilirubin (above about 2–2.5 mg/dl). Normal total bilirubin is 0.2–1.2 mg/dl. Jaundice is classified by the site of the defect.

1. Pre-hepatic (haemolytic) jaundice

  • Cause: excess breakdown of red cells – more bilirubin than the liver can conjugate
    • hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency
    • malaria, mismatched transfusion, Rh incompatibility, snake bite
  • Blood: unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin raised; anaemia, raised reticulocytes, raised LDH; liver enzymes normal
  • Urine: no bilirubin ("acholuric jaundice"); urobilinogen increased
  • Stool: dark (more stercobilin)

2. Hepatic (hepatocellular) jaundice

  • Cause: damage to liver cells – uptake, conjugation and excretion are all affected
    • viral hepatitis (A, B, C, E), alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis
    • drugs – paracetamol overdose, anti-tuberculosis drugs
    • leptospirosis, malaria; inherited (Gilbert's, Crigler–Najjar)
  • Blood: both conjugated and unconjugated raised – biphasic van den Bergh; ALT and AST very high; ALP mildly raised; low albumin and prolonged PT in severe disease
  • Urine: bilirubin present; urobilinogen normal or increased early
  • Stool: normal or pale

3. Post-hepatic (obstructive/cholestatic) jaundice

  • Cause: blockage of bile flow to the intestine
    • gallstones in the common bile duct
    • carcinoma head of pancreas, cholangiocarcinoma, bile duct stricture
    • enlarged lymph nodes at the porta hepatis; biliary atresia in infants
  • Blood: conjugated (direct) bilirubin raised; ALP and GGT very high; raised cholesterol; prolonged PT (vitamin K malabsorption) correctable with vitamin K
  • Urine: dark (bilirubin present); urobilinogen absent
  • Stool: pale, clay-coloured, bulky (fat malabsorption)
  • Itching (pruritus) due to bile salts

4. Comparison of findings

Finding Haemolytic Hepatocellular Obstructive
Serum bilirubin unconjugated ↑ both ↑ conjugated ↑
Van den Bergh indirect biphasic direct
Urine bilirubin absent present present
Urine urobilinogen increased variable absent
Stool colour dark normal/pale clay-coloured
ALT/AST normal very high mildly raised
ALP normal mildly raised very high

5. Nursing points

  • Observe colour of skin, sclera, urine and stool; record daily
  • Collect fresh urine for bilirubin and urobilinogen and protect from light
  • Relieve itching – cool baths, calamine, short nails
  • Watch for bleeding (prolonged PT); give vitamin K as ordered
  • Rest and adequate nutrition; avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs

Conclusion Jaundice is haemolytic, hepatocellular or obstructive; unconjugated bilirubin with excess urobilinogen suggests haemolysis, a biphasic pattern with very high transaminases suggests hepatitis, and conjugated bilirubin with absent urobilinogen, clay stools and high ALP suggests obstruction.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the glomerular function tests.
answer_html:
Introduction Glomerular function tests assess the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) – normally about 120 ml/min (above 90 ml/min/1.73 m²).

Tests

  1. Blood urea – 15–40 mg/dl (BUN 7–20 mg/dl)
  2. Serum creatinine – about 0.6–1.2 mg/dl (lower in women)
  3. Creatinine clearance – about 90–140 ml/min; needs a 24-hour urine collection with a blood sample
  4. Estimated GFR (eGFR) – calculated from serum creatinine, age and sex (CKD-EPI formula); used to stage chronic kidney disease
  5. Inulin clearance – the gold standard (research use)
  6. Cystatin C – a newer marker, independent of muscle mass
  7. Urea clearance – of historical value
  8. Radio-isotope GFR (DTPA scan)
  9. Urine protein/albumin – shows damage to the glomerular filter

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: List the liver function tests.
answer_html:
Introduction Liver function tests (LFTs) are a group of blood tests that assess different functions of the liver.

Tests grouped by function

  1. Excretory function – serum bilirubin (total, direct, indirect); urine bilirubin and urobilinogen
  2. Synthetic function – total protein, albumin, A:G ratio; prothrombin time (PT/INR)
  3. Liver cell injury – ALT (SGPT), AST (SGOT)
  4. Cholestasis – alkaline phosphatase (ALP), GGT, 5′-nucleotidase
  5. Metabolic / detoxification function – blood ammonia, blood glucose
  6. Special tests – viral markers (HBsAg, anti-HCV, IgM anti-HAV), alpha-fetoprotein (liver cancer), ceruloplasmin (Wilson's disease)

Uses: detect liver disease, distinguish hepatocellular from obstructive jaundice, assess severity (albumin, PT) and monitor hepatotoxic drugs such as anti-TB treatment.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Name the tubular function tests of the kidney.
answer_html:
Introduction Tubular function tests assess the ability of the renal tubules to reabsorb, secrete, concentrate and acidify urine.

Tests

  1. Urine specific gravity – normal 1.003–1.030; a fixed value around 1.010 indicates loss of concentrating ability
  2. Urine osmolality – 50–1,200 mOsm/kg; compared with plasma osmolality
  3. Urine concentration test (fluid deprivation) – a healthy kidney concentrates urine to specific gravity above about 1.025
  4. Urine dilution test (water load)
  5. Urine acidification test (ammonium chloride load) – for renal tubular acidosis
  6. Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) – below 1% in pre-renal failure, above 2% in tubular damage
  7. Tubular proteins and substances in urine – β₂-microglobulin, glucose with normal blood sugar, amino acids, phosphate (Fanconi syndrome)

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Why is serum creatinine a better indicator of kidney function than blood urea?
answer_html:
Reasons

  1. Creatinine is formed at a constant rate from muscle creatine, proportional to muscle mass
  2. It is not much affected by diet, while urea rises with high-protein diets
  3. It is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, so it reflects GFR closely; urea is partly reabsorbed, especially in dehydration
  4. Blood urea is also raised by GI bleeding, dehydration, fever, steroids and catabolic states, and lowered by liver disease – even when the kidneys are normal
  5. eGFR formulas use serum creatinine

Limitations of creatinine

  • Rises only after about 50% of kidney function is lost
  • Low in elderly and wasted patients with small muscle mass

BUN : creatinine ratio – normally 10–20 : 1; above 20 suggests pre-renal causes (dehydration, GI bleed).

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is hyperuricaemia? Give its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism. Hyperuricaemia is a serum uric acid above about 7 mg/dl in men and above 6 mg/dl in women (normal about 3.5–7.2 and 2.6–6 mg/dl).

Causes

  1. Increased production
    • purine-rich diet – organ meat, red meat, seafood; alcohol (beer)
    • increased cell turnover – leukaemia, lymphoma, psoriasis
    • chemotherapy (tumour lysis syndrome)
    • inherited enzyme defects (Lesch–Nyhan syndrome)
  2. Decreased excretion
    • kidney failure
    • drugs – thiazide diuretics, low-dose aspirin, pyrazinamide
    • lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, pre-eclampsia
  3. Obesity and metabolic syndrome

Effects: gout (painful joints, big toe), uric acid kidney stones, urate nephropathy.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Give the normal values of serum electrolytes.
answer_html:
Introduction Electrolytes are measured to assess fluid balance, kidney function and acid–base status.

Electrolyte Normal value
Sodium (Na⁺) 135–145 mEq/L
Potassium (K⁺) 3.5–5.0 mEq/L
Chloride (Cl⁻) 96–106 mEq/L
Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) 22–26 mEq/L
Calcium (total) 8.5–10.5 mg/dl (ionised about 4.5–5.3 mg/dl)
Phosphate 2.5–4.5 mg/dl
Magnesium 1.7–2.4 mg/dl

Points for nurses

  • Haemolysed samples falsely raise potassium – avoid prolonged tourniquet, fist clenching and vigorous shaking
  • Do not draw blood from an arm receiving an IV infusion
  • Report potassium below 3 or above 6 mEq/L urgently – risk of arrhythmia

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism?
answer_html:
Introduction Congenital hypothyroidism is deficiency of thyroid hormone from birth. If untreated it causes intellectual disability and poor growth (cretinism); it is one of the commonest preventable causes of intellectual disability. Most affected babies look normal at birth, so screening is essential.

Screening

  • A heel-prick blood sample is collected on filter paper (dried blood spot), ideally at 48–72 hours of age (or cord blood TSH)
  • TSH is measured; a raised TSH is confirmed by serum TSH and free T₄

Treatment

  • Levothyroxine started as early as possible – ideally within the first 2 weeks – gives normal development
  • Regular monitoring of thyroid tests and growth

Nurse's role: collect the sample correctly, record the baby's details, and ensure follow-up of positive results.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the renal function tests with their normal values and interpretation.
answer_html:
Introduction Renal (kidney) function tests (RFT/KFT) assess the kidneys' ability to filter blood, excrete waste, maintain fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance. They are used for diagnosis, monitoring and drug dosing.

A. Blood (biochemical) tests

Test Normal value Raised in
Blood urea 15–40 mg/dl kidney failure, dehydration, GI bleeding, high-protein diet
BUN 7–20 mg/dl as above
Serum creatinine 0.6–1.2 mg/dl kidney failure, muscle injury
Serum uric acid 3.5–7.2 mg/dl (men) kidney failure, gout
Sodium 135–145 mEq/L dehydration (falls in fluid overload)
Potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L kidney failure (danger)
Bicarbonate 22–26 mEq/L (falls in kidney failure – acidosis)
Calcium / phosphate 8.5–10.5 / 2.5–4.5 mg/dl phosphate rises and calcium falls in CKD

B. Clearance tests and eGFR

  • Creatinine clearance = (urine creatinine × urine volume per minute) ÷ plasma creatinine; normal about 90–140 ml/min
  • eGFR – calculated from creatinine, age and sex; used to stage chronic kidney disease (CKD):
    • G1 ≥90 (with kidney damage), G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 below 15 ml/min/1.73 m² (kidney failure)

C. Urine tests

  • Routine examination – volume, colour, specific gravity, pH, protein, sugar, ketones, blood, microscopy (RBC, pus cells, casts)
  • Protein: 24-hour urine protein or urine albumin–creatinine ratio (microalbuminuria – earliest sign of diabetic kidney disease)
  • Tubular tests – specific gravity, osmolality, concentration and acidification tests

D. Interpretation

  • Pre-renal failure (dehydration, shock) – BUN : creatinine above 20, concentrated urine, low urine sodium
  • Acute kidney injury – rapid rise of creatinine, fall in urine output
  • CKD – persistently low eGFR for more than 3 months, anaemia, high phosphate, low calcium, acidosis
  • Nephrotic syndrome – heavy proteinuria (above 3.5 g/day), low albumin, high cholesterol

E. Nursing responsibilities

  • Accurate 24-hour urine collection and intake–output charting
  • Avoid haemolysis (false high potassium)
  • Note nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, contrast media)
  • Daily weight; report rising creatinine or potassium

Conclusion Renal function is assessed by blood urea, creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes and urine examination; together they detect acute and chronic kidney disease, guide treatment and adjust drug doses.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the liver function tests with their normal values and interpretation.
answer_html:
Introduction The liver performs excretory, synthetic, metabolic and detoxifying functions. No single test measures all of them, so a group of tests (LFTs) is used to detect liver disease, find its type and assess its severity.

A. Tests of excretory function

  • Serum bilirubin – total 0.2–1.2 mg/dl; direct (conjugated) 0–0.3 mg/dl
    • raised in all types of jaundice; direct fraction raised in hepatitis and obstruction
  • Urine bilirubin (absent normally) and urobilinogen (traces)

B. Tests of synthetic function – show the severity and chronicity

  • Total protein 6–8 g/dl; albumin 3.5–5.0 g/dl
    • low albumin in chronic liver disease (cirrhosis) – half-life of albumin is about 20 days, so it falls slowly
  • Prothrombin time (PT) 11–13.5 seconds; INR about 1
    • prolonged in severe liver damage (acute or chronic) – an early sign of liver failure
    • if prolonged due to obstruction, it corrects with vitamin K; in liver cell damage it does not

C. Markers of liver cell injury

  • ALT 7–40 U/L and AST 5–40 U/L – very high in acute hepatitis; AST : ALT above 2 in alcoholic liver disease

D. Markers of cholestasis

  • ALP 40–130 U/L and GGT – very high in obstructive jaundice; GGT also rises with alcohol

E. Metabolic and detoxification tests

  • Blood ammonia – raised in liver failure (hepatic encephalopathy)
  • Blood glucose – hypoglycaemia in acute liver failure

F. Special tests

  • Viral markers – HBsAg (hepatitis B), anti-HCV, IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HEV
  • Alpha-fetoprotein – hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Autoantibodies, ceruloplasmin and copper (Wilson's disease)

G. Patterns

Condition Bilirubin ALT/AST ALP Albumin PT
Acute viral hepatitis ↑ ↑↑↑ ↑ normal normal or ↑
Obstructive jaundice ↑ (direct) ↑ ↑↑↑ normal ↑ (corrects with vitamin K)
Cirrhosis normal or ↑ mild ↑ mild ↑ ↓ ↑

H. Nursing responsibilities

  • No special fasting for most LFTs (fasting may be advised by some laboratories); avoid haemolysis
  • Note alcohol and drug history (paracetamol, anti-TB drugs)
  • Monitor patients on hepatotoxic drugs with periodic LFTs; check PT before invasive procedures such as liver biopsy

Conclusion LFTs combine bilirubin (excretion), albumin and PT (synthesis), ALT/AST (cell injury), ALP/GGT (cholestasis) and ammonia (detoxification); their pattern distinguishes hepatitis, obstruction and cirrhosis.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain the thyroid function tests and their interpretation.
answer_html:
Introduction Thyroid function tests (TFTs) measure thyroid hormones and the pituitary hormone TSH to diagnose and monitor hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism. The thyroid secretes mainly T₄ (thyroxine) and some T₃; most T₃ is formed from T₄ in tissues. In blood, more than 99% of the hormones are bound to proteins (TBG); only the free fraction is active.

A. Tests and normal values (vary with laboratory)

Test Approximate normal value
TSH 0.4–4.5 mIU/L
Free T₄ (FT₄) 0.8–1.8 ng/dl
Total T₄ 5–12 µg/dl
Free T₃ (FT₃) 2.3–4.2 pg/ml
Total T₃ 80–200 ng/dl
  • TSH is the best single screening test – it changes early and greatly in response to small changes in hormone levels

B. Interpretation

Condition TSH FT₄ / FT₃
Primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's, iodine deficiency, after thyroid surgery) high low
Subclinical hypothyroidism high normal
Primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic nodule) low (suppressed) high
T₃ toxicosis low FT₃ high, FT₄ normal
Subclinical hyperthyroidism low normal
Secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism low or normal low

C. Other thyroid tests

  • Anti-TPO antibodies – Hashimoto's thyroiditis
  • TSH-receptor antibodies – Graves' disease
  • Thyroglobulin – follow-up after treatment of thyroid cancer
  • Radioactive iodine uptake and scan – type of hyperthyroidism, nodules
  • Ultrasound and FNAC – thyroid swellings
  • Serum calcitonin – medullary carcinoma

D. Factors affecting results

  • Pregnancy and oral contraceptives raise TBG → total T₄ high but free T₄ normal; TSH targets in pregnancy are lower and trimester-specific
  • Drugs – amiodarone, lithium, steroids, iodine contrast
  • Severe illness may lower T₃ (sick euthyroid state)
  • Biotin supplements can interfere with some assays

E. Nursing responsibilities

  • Usually no fasting needed; record drugs and pregnancy
  • Teach patients to take levothyroxine on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast and not with calcium or iron tablets
  • Repeat TSH about 6–8 weeks after a dose change
  • Screen all newborns, and pregnant women as per guidelines

F. Common clinical pictures

  • Hypothyroidism – tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, menstrual problems, slow pulse
  • Hyperthyroidism – weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitation, sweating, anxiety, eye signs in Graves' disease

Conclusion TSH with free T₄ (and T₃) forms the core of thyroid function testing – high TSH with low T₄ means primary hypothyroidism and low TSH with high T₄/T₃ means hyperthyroidism – supported by antibody, scan and ultrasound studies.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Define antigen and antibody.
answer_html:
Antigen

  • An antigen is a substance that, when introduced into the body, stimulates an immune response and reacts specifically with the antibodies or cells produced
  • Usually proteins or polysaccharides of large size (molecular weight above about 10,000)
  • Examples – bacteria, viruses, toxins, ABO blood group substances, pollen, transplanted tissue
  • The small part of the antigen that binds the antibody is the epitope (antigenic determinant)
  • Hapten – a small molecule (e.g. penicillin) that becomes antigenic only when attached to a protein

Antibody

  • An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a glycoprotein produced by plasma cells (derived from B-lymphocytes) in response to an antigen, which combines specifically with that antigen
  • Five classes – IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD and IgE

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What are monoclonal antibodies? Give their uses.
answer_html:
Definition Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced by a single clone of B-cells; all are directed against one epitope of an antigen. They are made by hybridoma technology (Köhler and Milstein, 1975) – fusing an antibody-forming B-cell with a myeloma (cancer) cell, which can multiply indefinitely.

Uses

  1. Diagnosis
    • pregnancy test kits (hCG), ELISA and rapid card tests
    • blood grouping reagents, flow cytometry, tumour imaging
  2. Treatment (drug names end in "-mab")
    • cancer – trastuzumab (HER2-positive breast cancer), rituximab (lymphoma)
    • autoimmune diseases – infliximab, adalimumab (rheumatoid arthritis)
    • transplant rejection – basiliximab
    • infections – palivizumab (RSV in preterm infants)
  3. Research – identifying cell types and proteins

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What are tumour markers? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Tumour markers are substances produced by tumour cells (or by the body in response to a tumour) that can be measured in blood, urine or tissue – usually by immunoassay.

Examples

Marker Cancer
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) hepatocellular carcinoma, germ-cell tumours
CEA colorectal cancer
CA-125 ovarian cancer
CA 19-9 pancreatic cancer
PSA prostate cancer
β-hCG choriocarcinoma, hydatidiform mole, testicular tumours
CA 15-3 breast cancer
Calcitonin medullary carcinoma of thyroid

Uses: monitoring treatment and detecting recurrence (main use), supporting diagnosis, screening in selected cases (PSA).

Limitation: may be raised in non-cancer conditions and normal in early cancer.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Differentiate between primary and secondary antibody responses.
answer_html:
Point Primary response Secondary (booster/anamnestic) response
Occurs on first exposure to an antigen repeat exposure to the same antigen
Lag period long (about 7–10 days) short (1–3 days)
Antibody level low high (10–100 times more)
Main antibody IgM IgG
Duration short-lived long-lasting
Affinity of antibody low high
Cells responding naive B-cells memory B-cells

Significance

  • Explains the need for booster doses of vaccines (e.g. tetanus toxoid)
  • IgM antibody indicates recent infection; IgG indicates past infection or immunity

Example: a person who completed tetanus vaccination gets a quick, strong IgG response to a booster dose of Td after an injury.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: What is the principle of the urine pregnancy card test?
answer_html:
Principle

  • The test detects human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a hormone made by the placenta (syncytiotrophoblast) after implantation
  • It is an immunochromatographic (lateral-flow) sandwich immunoassay – urine flows along a strip containing monoclonal anti-hCG antibodies labelled with coloured particles (colloidal gold)
  • If hCG is present, the complex is captured at the test line (T); excess label is captured at the control line (C)

Reading

  • Two lines (C and T) – positive
  • Only C line – negative
  • No C line – invalid; repeat with a new kit

Practical points

  • Becomes positive about 10–14 days after conception (around the missed period)
  • Use first morning urine (most concentrated)
  • False positive – recent abortion or delivery, hCG injections, molar pregnancy; false negative – testing too early, dilute urine
  • The Nischay pregnancy test kit is supplied free through ASHAs for early registration of pregnancy

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Describe the structure and functions of immunoglobulins.
answer_html:
Introduction Immunoglobulins (Ig) are glycoproteins that function as antibodies. They are produced by plasma cells (activated B-lymphocytes) and form the gamma-globulin fraction of plasma proteins. They provide humoral immunity.

A. Basic structure (IgG as the model)

  1. A Y-shaped molecule made of four polypeptide chains:
    • two identical heavy (H) chains – about 440 amino acids each
    • two identical light (L) chains – about 220 amino acids each; either kappa (κ) or lambda (λ)
  2. Chains are held together by disulphide bonds
  3. Each chain has a variable (V) region at the tip and a constant (C) region
    • the variable regions of one heavy and one light chain form the antigen-binding site (hypervariable regions give specificity)
    • the constant region of the heavy chain decides the class of antibody
  4. Hinge region – gives flexibility to the arms
  5. Enzyme papain splits the molecule into:
    • two Fab fragments – bind antigen
    • one Fc fragment – binds complement and Fc receptors on phagocytes; responsible for placental transfer
  6. IgM (pentamer) and secretory IgA (dimer) also contain a J chain; secretory IgA has a secretory component

B. Classes and functions

Class Heavy chain Form Share of serum Ig Main features
IgG γ monomer about 75–80% only Ig that crosses the placenta; main antibody of secondary response; neutralises toxins; activates complement
IgA α monomer (serum), dimer (secretions) 10–15% mucosal immunity; present in colostrum, breast milk, saliva, tears, gut and respiratory secretions
IgM μ pentamer (largest) 5–10% first antibody formed (primary response); best activator of complement; ABO antibodies; IgM in a newborn indicates intrauterine infection
IgD δ monomer below 1% B-cell surface receptor
IgE ε monomer trace binds mast cells and basophils – allergy, anaphylaxis, asthma; defence against worms

C. General functions of antibodies

  1. Neutralisation of toxins and viruses
  2. Opsonisation – coating microbes for phagocytosis
  3. Complement activation – lysis of bacteria
  4. Agglutination and precipitation of antigens
  5. Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (killing by NK cells)
  6. Mucosal protection (IgA)
  7. Passive immunity to the fetus (IgG) and infant (IgA in breast milk)

D. Clinical relevance

  • Colostrum feeding protects newborns
  • Immunoglobulin injections – anti-rabies, anti-tetanus, hepatitis B immunoglobulin, anti-D after delivery of an Rh-positive baby to an Rh-negative mother
  • Raised IgE in allergy and worm infestation; monoclonal increase in myeloma

Conclusion Immunoglobulins are Y-shaped glycoproteins of two heavy and two light chains, with Fab regions binding antigen and an Fc region performing effector functions; the five classes – IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD and IgE – provide humoral immunity, passive protection and allergic responses.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain ELISA – principle, types, procedure and interpretation.
answer_html:
Introduction ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) is a highly sensitive laboratory test that detects and measures antigens or antibodies in blood and other fluids. It is widely used for HIV, hepatitis B and C, dengue and hormone testing.

A. Principle

  • An antigen–antibody reaction takes place on a solid surface (plastic microtitre wells)
  • One of the reactants is linked to an enzyme (e.g. horseradish peroxidase or alkaline phosphatase)
  • When a substrate is added, the enzyme converts it into a coloured product
  • The intensity of colour (optical density measured by an ELISA reader) is proportional to the amount of antigen or antibody

B. Types

  1. Direct ELISA – enzyme-labelled antibody binds directly to antigen coated on the well
  2. Indirect ELISA – detects antibodies in patient serum; antigen is coated, patient antibody binds, then an enzyme-labelled anti-human antibody is added – e.g. HIV antibody, anti-HCV
  3. Sandwich ELISA – detects antigens; antigen is "sandwiched" between a capture antibody and an enzyme-labelled detection antibody – e.g. HBsAg, dengue NS1, hormones
  4. Competitive ELISA – patient antigen competes with labelled antigen; colour is inversely proportional – small molecules such as hormones and drugs

C. Procedure (indirect ELISA)

  1. Coating – wells coated with known antigen
  2. Blocking – unoccupied sites blocked with protein
  3. Add patient serum and controls → incubate → wash
  4. Add enzyme-labelled conjugate (anti-human Ig) → incubate → wash
  5. Add substrate (e.g. TMB) → colour develops
  6. Stop the reaction with acid
  7. Read optical density in the ELISA reader (e.g. at 450 nm)

D. Interpretation

  • Results are compared with a cut-off value calculated from controls
  • OD above cut-off – reactive; below – non-reactive; near cut-off – equivocal, repeat
  • A reactive screening test must be confirmed – e.g. HIV is diagnosed only after testing with different kits as per the national (NACO) testing strategy
  • Window period – early infection may give a false-negative result

E. Advantages

  • High sensitivity and specificity; many samples tested together; can be automated
  • No radioactivity (unlike RIA); reagents are stable

F. Limitations

  • False positives (cross-reacting antibodies) and false negatives (window period)
  • Needs trained staff, equipment and 2–3 hours

G. Uses

  • Infections – HIV, hepatitis B and C, dengue (NS1, IgM), typhoid, scrub typhus
  • Hormones – TSH, hCG; tumour markers; autoantibodies; drug levels; food allergens
  • Screening of donated blood

H. Nursing responsibilities

  • Pre-test and post-test counselling and consent for HIV testing; maintain confidentiality
  • Collect blood in a plain tube, label correctly, avoid haemolysis
  • Follow standard precautions while handling samples

Conclusion ELISA uses an enzyme-labelled antigen–antibody reaction that produces colour in proportion to the amount of antigen or antibody; its direct, indirect, sandwich and competitive forms are used for diagnosing infections, measuring hormones and screening blood.

subject: Applied Biochemistry
question: Explain antigen–antibody reactions and their use in diagnosis.
answer_html:
Introduction Antigen–antibody reactions are the specific combination of an antigen with its corresponding antibody. They are the basis of serological tests used to detect infections, blood groups, hormones and diseases.

A. Characteristics

  1. Specific – an antibody reacts only with its own antigen
  2. Binding is non-covalent and reversible
  3. Optimal proportions are needed – in great antibody excess (prozone) the test may be falsely negative (e.g. VDRL in secondary syphilis); the sample is then diluted
  4. Can be measured qualitatively and quantitatively (titre)

B. Types of reactions and their uses

1. Precipitation – soluble antigen + antibody → visible precipitate

  • VDRL test (flocculation) – syphilis screening; immunodiffusion

2. Agglutination – particulate antigen (cells) + antibody → clumping

  • ABO and Rh blood grouping and cross-matching
  • Widal test – typhoid
  • Coombs' test – haemolytic disease of the newborn, autoimmune haemolysis
  • Latex agglutination – CRP, rheumatoid factor, ASO

3. Complement fixation – the reaction uses up complement; once used for syphilis (Wassermann test), now rarely used

4. Neutralisation – antibodies neutralise toxins and viruses; basis of antitoxin therapy (tetanus, diphtheria antitoxin)

5. Immunofluorescence – antibodies labelled with fluorescent dye seen under a fluorescence microscope

  • antinuclear antibodies (ANA) in SLE; rabies antigen detection

6. Immunoassays with labels

  • ELISA – enzyme label (HIV, HBsAg, dengue)
  • CLIA (chemiluminescence immunoassay) – hormones, tumour markers, troponin
  • RIA – radioactive label (now rarely used)

7. Immunochromatography (rapid card tests)

  • Quick bedside point-of-care tests using coloured-particle-labelled antibodies on a strip
  • e.g. malaria (bivalent RDT), dengue NS1/IgM, HIV, HBsAg, syphilis, urine pregnancy test

8. Western blot – identifies antibodies against specific separated proteins; once a confirmatory test for HIV

9. Flow cytometry – counts cells labelled with fluorescent antibodies – CD4 count in HIV

C. Advantages in diagnosis

  • Specific, sensitive, mostly simple, and some give results in minutes at the bedside

D. Nursing responsibilities

  • Correct sample (serum/whole blood), labelling and timely transport
  • Blood grouping and cross-matching – correct patient identification to prevent transfusion reactions
  • Perform rapid tests (malaria, pregnancy, HIV under programme guidelines) correctly and record results
  • Maintain confidentiality and standard precautions

Conclusion Antigen–antibody reactions – precipitation, agglutination, neutralisation, immunofluorescence and labelled immunoassays such as ELISA and rapid card tests – form the basis of blood grouping, serological diagnosis of infections and measurement of hormones and tumour markers.
